HALLMARK: How to Diagnose LLM Citation Verifiers and When to Deploy Them

Kayoon Kim Affiliation: University of Tübingen Affiliation: ELLIS Institute Tübingen Email: kyoonkm@gmail.com    Wieland Brendel Affiliation: ELLIS Institute Tübingen Affiliation: Max Planck Institute for Intelligent Systems    Patrik Reizinger Affiliation: ELLIS Institute Tübingen Affiliation: Max Planck Institute for Intelligent Systems
Abstract

GPTZero found 53 NeurIPS 2025 accepted papers with hallucinated citations (Shmatko et al., 2026; Ansari, 2026), and venues now screen submissions with automated reference checkers. Rule- and Large Language Model (LLM)-based verifiers are emerging, but many are released without a shared evaluation and each flags a different kind of error, so it is unclear which to trust or when to deploy them. We address this with Hallmark (Hallucination benchmark): 2,526 BibTeX entries spanning 14 hallucination types, with per-type and diagnostic sub-test labels and further temporal, cross-domain, and real-world evaluation splits. We evaluate zero-shot and tool-augmented LLMs, a DOI-lookup baseline, and our own co-designed rule-based verifier, bibtex-updater. Verifiers can miss hallucinations and wrongly flag correct papers, so every flag still needs human review. The false positive rate (FPR) determines the review effort and thus limits deployment. The tested models exhibit an order-of-magnitude spread in FPR; agentic lookups buy recall but inflate FPR, and neither smaller models nor prompt optimization reach the frontier’s operating point. A two-stage cascade with bibtex-updater avoids that inflation, providing an upper bound, given the co-design. These rankings, however, depend on what counts as a hallucination: re-scoring the types that describe a real work cited inaccurately changes which verifier ranks first, and venues have not agreed on a definition. We call for a community definition and release per-type labels and a re-scoring protocol so that any agreed definition can be scored against every verifier.
††footnotetext: Benchmark and code: https://github.com/rpatrik96/hallmark; verification tool (bibtex-updater): https://github.com/rpatrik96/bibtexupdater.

1 Introduction

Hallucinated citations—fabricated references generated by language models—have become a prevalent threat to scientific publishing, especially because they often seem plausible. Shortly after NeurIPS 2025, GPTZero audited the 4,841 accepted papers and found 53 with fabricated citations that had passed peer review (Shmatko et al., 2026; Ansari, 2026), and independent audits report hundreds more across venues and a sharp rise since 2021 (Xu et al., 2026; Sakai et al., 2026a; Bienz et al., 2026). Venues now screen submissions for them: ICLR 2026 ran an automated reference checker, desk-rejected papers with confirmed hallucinations, and reported a significant false-positive rate (ICLR, 2026).

Verifiers have multiplied, from DOI resolvers to multi-database cross-referencing systems and LLM-based checkers. Many are released without a shared evaluation, and often focus on different error types, ranging from records that cannot be found to mismatched authors, venue or year. It is unclear which to trust, or how to deploy them.

To enable comparisons and to provide practical guidance on deployment for authors and venues, we release Hallmark, comprising 2,526 BibTeX entries spanning 14 hallucination types across three difficulty tiers, with taxonomy labels and six diagnostic sub-tests. We evaluate a DOI-lookup baseline, frontier and small LLMs zero-shot, tool-augmented agents, and our own rule-based verifier bibtex-updater, which was co-designed with the taxonomy and is therefore reported as an upper bound rather than ranked. We score every verifier under a single protocol (Fig. 1) and rely on both a held-out test set and four additional evaluation-only splits that add recent papers, a second domain, and authentic ChatGPT citations.

Scope.

Hallmark targets citation metadata—detecting fabricated, inconsistent, or nonexistent bibliographic records—not claim-level hallucination, which needs full-text analysis.

Current citation verifiers are not perfect; thus, human review is required, and the false-positive rate, not recall, becomes the bottleneck for deployment, as we show in our positive predictive value (PPV) analysis in § 4.4, with FPR spanning an order of magnitude (0.0430.043 to 0.7020.702). We observe and analyze three failure modes (Tab. 20): (i) agentic lookups buy recall but inflate FPR; (ii) precision collapses at realistic prevalence; and (iii) most LLMs by default over-flag papers published after their training cutoff. Some of these failure modes can be mitigated: a two-stage cascade with bibtex-updater avoids inflating FPR by passing only uncertain entries to an LLM. It catches nearly all hallucinations at a low false-positive rate, which we treat as an upper bound given the co-design. A prompt that reminds the model of its training cutoff (i.e., cutoff-aware) reduces over-flagging of recent papers, but mostly through abstention; mitigating it selectively is left for future work. Prompt optimization (Agrawal et al., 2026) also has limits, especially for smaller models, which maintain high FPR.

Verifier performance and ranking depend on the—perhaps surprisingly ambiguous—definition of a hallucination. For example, a real work cited with the wrong venue is not fully correct, but is that a hallucination? Existing verifiers address this differently in what they check, and venues have not (yet) reached consensus. We therefore urge the community to have more discussion on definitions of hallucinated citations; meanwhile, we release per-type labels and a re-scoring protocol so that any agreed definition can be scored against every verifier.

Our contributions are:

  1. 1.

    A benchmark and taxonomy for citation-hallucination detection, with per-type and sub-test labels and temporal, cross-domain, and real-world splits (§ 3).

  2. 2.

    A failure-mode analysis of citation verifiers under one protocol, showing that the false-positive rate decides deployability (§ 4.4).

  3. 3.

    A re-scoring protocol that lets any definition of a hallucinated citation be applied to every verifier.

2 Related work

Citation hallucination in the LLM era.

LLM hallucination (Ji et al., 2023; Huang et al., 2025) manifests distinctly in citations (Alkaissi & McFarlane, 2023; Agrawal et al., 2024; Walters & Wilder, 2023); venue-level audits document scale—GhostCite (Xu et al., 2026) on 56K papers, HalluCitation (Sakai et al., 2026a) on ACL/NAACL/EMNLP, the HPC-venue study of Bienz et al. (2026), and CITADEL’s audit of 2.5 million PubMed Central papers (Topaz et al., 2026)—measuring prevalence, not detection-tool performance. Detection tools—HaRC (HaRC Contributors, 2024), verify-citations (verify-citations Contributors, 2025), RefChecker (Hu et al., 2024), CheckIfExist (Abbonato, 2026)—report incompatible metrics on disjoint test data, preventing direct comparison; CheckIfExist (a CrossRef/Semantic-Scholar/OpenAlex cascade verifier) ships without dataset or metrics, and RefChecker requires full-text manuscript context. Concurrent work (Rao & Callison-Burch, 2026; Rao et al., 2026; Sakai et al., 2026b) evaluates LLM-as-citation-generator accuracy or releases lightweight checkers. The closest work to Hallmark is CiteAudit (Shi et al., 2026), which likewise benchmarks LLMs and commercial verifiers on a human-validated/annotated dataset via a multi-agent pipeline. Hallmark differs by focusing on understanding failure modes by rich diagnostics. It provides a 14-type, tier-stratified error taxonomy and post-cutoff evaluation splits that expose training-cutoff effects, so it reports which metadata failures each tool catches. Adjacent concurrent detection work (Rao et al., 2026) targets citation-URL liveness on DRBench (the stale-vs-hallucinated distinction), a scope orthogonal to Hallmark’s BibTeX-metadata cross-consistency checks. § C.7 details boundary cases of audit-vs-benchmark categorization.

Hallucination detection benchmarks.

General-purpose hallucination benchmarks (Li et al., 2023; Ravichander et al., 2025) target factual claims, not metadata; adjacent work—FactScore (Min et al., 2023), RARR (Gao et al., 2023), SciFact (Wadden et al., 2020)—does not evaluate BibTeX integrity (Digital Object Identifier (DOI)/title/author/venue cross-consistency against external databases). Concurrent generator-side benchmarks such as HalluHard (Fan et al., 2026) measure whether LLMs produce claims grounded by retrievable inline citations in multi-turn dialogs. None evaluates the verifiers that check citation metadata. Hallmark’s design borrows from established benchmarks: temporal segmentation, as in SWE-bench (Jimenez et al., 2024) and LiveCodeBench (Jain et al., 2025), separates recall from verification, and multi-criteria sub-tests, as in HumanEval (Chen et al., 2021), attribute each failure to a field (§ C.7).

3 The Hallmark benchmark

3.1 Hallucination taxonomy

We define 14 citation hallucination types—11 empirically grounded and 3 stress-test types—organized into three difficulty tiers based on the verification effort required (Tab. 2, in the appendix). Tier 1 (Easy) hallucinations are settled by one check, a single lookup (fabricated_doi, nonexistent_venue) or none at all (placeholder_authors, future_date). Tier 2 (Medium) hallucinations require cross-referencing multiple metadata fields: e.g., chimeric_title pairs real authors with a fabricated title, wrong_venue assigns a paper to the wrong conference, and hybrid_fabrication uses a real DOI whose resolved record does not match the BibTeX metadata. Tier 3 (Hard) hallucinations require deep verification or semantic reasoning: near_miss_title entries differ by one or two words from a real paper; plausible_fabrication entries are entirely invented but realistic; and arxiv_version_mismatch entries cite a preprint with wrong venue and shifted year. The tiers rank the effort a human verifier needs, not difficulty for an LLM.

The taxonomy is grounded in real incidents: we derived it from hallucinated citations in the NeurIPS 2025 incident and related audits (Xu et al., 2026; Sakai et al., 2026a), then stress-tested it with adversarial brainstorming of failure modes existing tools might miss. Of the 108 real-world hallucinated citations in the benchmark, the 72 we analyzed in detail map cleanly to a single type 79% of the time, with the rest assigned to their highest applicable tier (§ A.2). Three types—merged_citation, partial_author_list, arxiv_version_mismatch—we could not trace to a documented incident, so we treat them as stress-test types. They appear in every split (18.3% of hallucinated entries on dev_public, 20.2% on test_public); per-type labels let each type be scored separately. Perturbation rules, generation prompts and the collection procedure are in §§ A.3 and B.2.3.

3.2 Dataset construction

The dataset contains two classes of entries: valid references scraped from DBLP and hallucinated references built with the four methods below.

Valid entries.

We scraped BibTeX records from DBLP (dblp Team, 2025) for papers published at major ML venues (NeurIPS, ICML, ICLR, AAAI, CVPR) between 2021 and 2023, plus 35 arXiv preprints from February 2026 (22 dev_public, 13 test_public) as a recency probe. Each entry was verified by confirming DOI resolution where a DOI is present (46%46\% of valid entries), title existence in at least two databases, and author-venue consistency. This retained 1,036 valid entries.

Hallucinated entries.

We generated hallucinated entries using four methods: Systematic perturbation: modifying specific fields of valid entries to produce targeted hallucination types (e.g., replacing a DOI with a non-resolving one for fabricated_doi, swapping author lists between papers for swapped_authors). LLM generation: prompting language models to generate plausible but fictional references for types requiring coherent fabrication (plausible_fabrication, chimeric_title). Adversarial crafting: manually constructing entries designed to evade specific detection strategies. Real-world collection: harvesting actual hallucinated citations from published papers identified in audits. An evaluation-only supplement of 341 authentic ChatGPT-generated citations (172 valid / 169 hallucinated), hand-verified by Walters & Wilder (2023) across 42 multidisciplinary topics, adds real-world hallucinations (§ C.6).

Labeling.

Labels are assigned deterministically by the generation pipeline; LLM-generated entries are also filtered against bibliographic databases, and real-world and adversarial entries receive manual review (§ A.3).

Splits and release.

Every hallucinated entry is built by modifying some real base paper. Across the two public splits those base papers do not overlap: no hallucinated entry on one split is built from a paper that appears as a valid entry on the other. test_hidden and stress_test do not have this property: 109 of their 244 and 68 of their 121 hallucinated entries modify a paper that is a valid entry in public data. Most types on dev_public and test_public carry ≥30\geq 30 instances, enough for meaningful per-type comparison; test_hidden spreads 244 hallucinated entries over 14 types and does not clear that floor, so its per-type intervals are wider (statistical power in § B.1).

Every entry passes automated validation, the url field is blinded to avoid using URL resolution as a shortcut for verification, unique marker tokens in the metadata expose memorization if a model reproduces one, and types are roughly balanced to maximize per-type power (§ A.3). The core splits are dev_public (1,119 entries), test_public (831), test_hidden (454), and stress_test (122); per-split counts and the four evaluation-only splits are in Tab. 5. Entries carry a temporal segment tag (pre-2023, 2023–2024, 2025+), used for the post-cutoff analysis in §§ 4.4 and F.

Sub-test design.

To understand what is hallucinated and why, each entry decomposes citation validity into six independently verifiable dimensions, each scored True/False/N/A: DOI resolves, Title exists in bibliographic databases, Authors match the identified paper, Venue real and correctly attributed, Fields complete, Cross-DB agreement.

The six sub-tests also make an entry’s defect count observable: one type can span several failed sub-tests, and multi-defect entries are the norm in the real-world subset, whereas under perturbation they are rare. Detection by defect count is in § C.5.3.

4 Experiments

4.1 Metrics

Our comparison focuses on two prevalence-independent metrics, ensuring they remain comparable across splits with differing class ratios. Detection rate (DR) is recall on the hallucinated class; FPR is the fraction of valid entries wrongly flagged. Tier-weighted F1 (TW-F1) weights each hallucinated entry by its tier (1/2/3), rewarding the detection of harder hallucinations. Matthews Correlation Coefficient (MCC) reads all four confusion-matrix cells; it moves with prevalence by ≤0.03{\leq}0.03 between our splits (54.2%54.2\% vs. 62.5%62.5\% hallucinated). Expected Calibration Error (ECE) (Naeini et al., 2015) measures how well a tool’s confidence tracks its accuracy; an ECE below 0.050.05 is excellent and above 0.20.2 unreliable. Formal definitions are in § B.1; per-tier and per-type breakdowns in §§ 4.3 and C.4.

4.2 Evaluated tools

We evaluate thirteen independent full-coverage tools (i.e., returning a verdict on every entry, neither co-designed with the benchmark nor given tool access) on dev_public: a DOI-only lower bound and twelve zero-shot LLMs from OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, Meta, Mistral, DeepSeek and Qwen (Tab. 1; model IDs in § B.2.4), including a later-cutoff GPT-5.4 control (Aug 2025 cutoff) for § 4.4. All LLMs use the same zero-shot prompt at temperature 00 and seed 4242 with one API call per entry; DeepSeek-R1’s chain-of-thought raises its median latency to ∼19{\sim}19 s against 11–1010 s for the single-pass cohort (Tab. 19). On top of these, four agentic variants (§ B.2.4) allow up to five database lookups per entry; prompted to cross-reference databases, the model tends to flag an entry as soon as one lookup returns no match—the disposition behind the inflated false-positive rate we report in § 4.4. HaRC (HaRC Contributors, 2024) and verify-citations (verify-citations Contributors, 2025) are excluded from Tab. 1: neither returns its own verdicts at benchmark scale, so any row for them would report the shared pre-screening layer (§ B.2.2). The DOI-only baseline only verifies each entry’s DOI against the DOI.org resolver. The optional pre-screening layer (DOI format, year bounds, author heuristics) is applied to the database-lookup tools and the cascade, not to the LLM verifiers, so those rows include their verdicts (§§ 4.4 and D.1). We label bibtex-updater co-designed because its development overlapped the taxonomy: the typed sub-tests partly mirror the tool’s verification stages, so it may score better here than on a novel hallucination distribution. We read its row as an unranked upper-bound reference (§ G.2).

4.3 Main results

Scoring conventions.

Rows in Tab. 1—which reports dev_public—are ranked by point estimate, with a paired test only where per-entry predictions allow (§ B.1); an LLM’s uncertain verdicts are excluded from the DR/FPR/F1 triple, while bibtex-updater resolves its abstentions to valid before scoring (§§ B.1 and E.2); predictions were collected 2026-05-05 apart from the two rows marked § in Tab. 1, from a later collection (2026-09-02), and hosted-LLM rows are dated snapshots subject to endpoint drift (§ 5).

LLMs span a wide recall–precision spectrum.

The FPR ordering of Tab. 1 (DR vs. FPR tradeoff in Fig. 2) runs from models that flag rarely (Gemini 2.5 Pro) to models that flag most entries (DeepSeek-V3.2). The two later-cutoff Anthropic models give the best balance—Opus 4.7 and Sonnet 4.6 have the highest F1 and the best calibration of the independent tools, at a middling FPR. Their F1 gap is only 0.3 pp (paired bootstrap p=0.74p{=}0.74, § B.1), and it reverses direction between the May and September runs: Opus 4.7 leads on the 2026-05-05 run, Sonnet 4.6 on the 2026-09-02 one (Tab. 29). Neither model beats the other on both axes—Opus 4.7 has the lower FPR (.154.154 vs. .161.161), Sonnet 4.6 the higher recall (.916.916 vs. .906.906)—and on the earlier 2026-05-05 collection both sat at the low-FPR end (.072.072, .127.127; Tab. 29). Sonnet’s extra recall is also partly over-flagging: of the 27 dev_public papers the ground-truth audit reclassified as real (§ 3.2), Sonnet flagged 19 as hallucinated and Opus 8. Both clear GPT-5.1 and the open-weight models that flag most entries, and GPT-5.4 (cutoff Aug 2025) sits between them at lower FPR and comparable recall, consistent with § 4.4.

§ E.2 examines whether bibtex-updater’s low FPR depends on abstention. Because DR and FPR are prevalence-independent, we compare on them, and on F1 only within a split.

Per-type analysis.

Per-type detection rates (heatmap in Fig. 3; full table in Tab. 13) show the same pattern across models: most LLMs catch nearly every Tier-1 hallucination, while swapped_authors and near_miss_title are the hardest types for almost every model. GPT-5.1 reaches at least 74% on 9 of 11 main types and is perfect on nonexistent_venue and placeholder_authors. Its two weak types, swapped_authors and near_miss_title, both turn on exact bibliographic knowledge and map to the Authors match and Title exists sub-tests respectively (§ 3.2; Tab. 2).

Small models.

As not every researcher can access the largest (and, often, costliest) models, we investigate whether a small local model can be a good substitute. We test on Claude Haiku 4.5 and four Qwen3 open-weight models at 4, 8, 14 and 32B, under the same protocol as Tab. 1, and report the details in § C.3. Haiku performs substantially worse than the tested Anthropic Sonnet and Opus models, and the smaller open-weight models flag more than 95%95\% of the split as hallucinations, yielding a high DR carrying no information: at venue-realistic prevalence their PPV is indistinguishable from the base rate (§ E.1), so nearly every entry requires manual checks. Thus, cheap inference does not make deployment cheap.

Cross-split robustness.

The held-out test_public (831 entries) tells a complementary story to the dev_public results (Δ\DeltaFPR in Tab. 1; full results in § C.1). Among standalone tools with DR ≥0.80{\geq}0.80, bibtex-updater keeps the lowest false-positive rate on both splits (0.0510.051 on dev_public, 0.0800.080 on test_public), which we read as an upper bound given the co-design; out of domain its FPR stays low but its coverage drops (§ G.2).

Prompt sensitivity.

A prompt-sensitivity ablation on 150 dev_public entries (four prompt variants, four models; § H.2) moves the same model’s absolute FPR by 1010–3737 pp on wording alone, while the model ranking barely moves (mean pairwise Spearman rank correlation ρ=0.90\rho{=}0.90): absolute FPR values depend on the prompt, the model ordering does not.

4.4 Failure modes

Three failure modes recur across the cohort (Tab. 20); we diagnose each in turn.

Agentic lookups give diminishing returns (failure mode (i)).

Five tool calls push GPT-5.1’s recall past bibtex-updater’s, but its false-positive rate rises to roughly nine times bibtex-updater’s, because the prompted model—cross-referencing against CrossRef/OpenAlex/arXiv—tends to flag an entry as soon as one of them returns no match. The inflation is a property of the harness—its naive, single-stage use of the lookups—not of the base model or of tool access itself: swapping Sonnet 4.6 for GPT-5.1 reproduces the profile within ≤5{\leq}5 pp on every metric, and Sonnet’s FPR rises ∼3.4×{\sim}3.4{\times} over its zero-shot baseline from the same collection, while GPT-5.1’s already-high zero-shot FPR barely changes. This any-no-match policy fails because CrossRef, OpenAlex, and arXiv have partial, non-overlapping coverage: a real paper is routinely missing from one of them, so single-source absence gets read as fabrication. A better alternative is to flag only on consensus absence across sources (or on positive metadata inconsistency) and to route single-source absence to uncertain/human review (§ E.2); § 4.5 measures that policy. A deterministic re-aggregation over three of the harness’s four databases confirms improvement (Appx. D), so failure mode (i) characterizes a retrieval-augmented pattern, not an inherent shortcoming of agentic systems. Tool access therefore trades precision for recall: agentic harnesses flag an entry as soon as one database misses it.

Precision at low prevalence (failure mode (ii)).

Precision (PPV, the fraction of flags that are genuine hallucinations) falls at low prevalence by Bayes’ rule (§ E.1). Our analysis focuses on how verifiers compare, given the wide range of FPR in Tab. 1, from 0.0430.043 to 0.7020.702. At a venue-realistic ∼2%{\sim}2\% base rate that becomes a ∼6×{\sim}6{\times} gap in precision: the best verifiers catch one true hallucination per 6–10 flags, the most aggressive fewer than one in 35, even at ≥87%{\geq}87\% detection (per-tool PPV in Tab. 23, sweep in Tab. 24). Calibration does not simply follow FPR: Sonnet 4.6 and Opus 4.7 are the best-calibrated zero-shot LLMs (ECE 0.0410.041, 0.0520.052) at a middling FPR, while the lowest-FPR model, Gemini 2.5 Pro, is among the worst calibrated (0.2970.297). The co-designed bibtex-updater has a low FPR because it flags conservatively rather than abstaining, and reaches one-in-four precision (§ E.2). The optional pre-screening layer adds ∼5{\sim}5 pp overall (∼18{\sim}18 pp on Tier 1); we report numbers with and without pre-screening. Every metric from which abstentions are excluded is paired with its coverage and an aggressive re-scoring that scores every abstention as hallucinated (§ E.2), so deferring hard cases cannot improve low precision.

Prevalence (the base rate of hallucinated entries) moves deployability while leaving the ranking fixed. Sweeping the base rate over 11–5%5\% leaves the PPV ordering essentially fixed (Tab. 24), because prevalence cancels from pairwise comparisons. Thus, the DR/FPR ratio determines the ranking; however, the base rate affects absolute precision: at a 2%2\% base rate even the best independent verifier (Gemini 2.5 Pro) reaches only ∼16%{\sim}16\% PPV. Still, depending on prevalence, the cost ratio cFN/cFPc_{\text{FN}}/c_{\text{FP}}, and reviewer capacity, it might be worth ranking based on recall. We discuss the different deployment considerations and regimes in § E.3.

Temporal robustness (failure mode (iii)).

A separate 448-entry supplement disjoint from the 2021–2023 corpus (300 valid 2024–2025 DBLP entries, 148 hallucinated; § F.1) shows LLM verifiers degrade sharply beyond their training cutoff. The earlier-cutoff models default to “flag everything unfamiliar”: F1 falls to ≈0.55{\approx}0.55 as false positives inflate, with GPT-5.1’s FPR alone rising 41.1%→75.9%41.1\%{\to}75.9\%. DeepSeek-R1’s detection rate is not evaluable: API error fallbacks took 151 of its 448 entries, all 148 hallucinated ones among them; on the valid entries it answered, FPR =0.856{=}0.856 (full panel: Tab. 28). As with every absolute FPR here, these values depend on the prompt, so we read them through the model ordering (Prompt sensitivity, § 4.3). Retrieval need not help: databases also lag on recent papers (§ F.2).

Later-cutoff resistance. Only the two latest-cutoff Anthropic models hold their false-positive rate near in-distribution levels (Sonnet 4.6 12.0%12.0\%, Opus 4.7 7.3%7.3\%); Gemini 2.5 Pro and GPT-5.4 (Tab. 31) over-flag only moderately, and the remaining eight degrade sharply to 59.559.5–88.7%88.7\% (the “over-flagging cluster”; Tab. 28). The two Anthropic models’ dev→\totemporal FPR barely moves (−0.7-0.7 and +0.1+0.1 pp). Both figures in that comparison come from the May experiment, since a shift across the cutoff is only interpretable within one endpoint snapshot; the September re-run of these two models reported in Tab. 1 puts their dev_public FPR higher (.161.161, .154.154), a drift larger than the temporal shift itself (we provide more details about endpoint drift in Tab. 29). We report this as a descriptive pattern, not a calibration result, because the design cannot cleanly separate two explanations: the valid pool is scraped from DBLP and these are the latest-cutoff models in the cohort, so a low FPR on a valid entry is indistinguishable from training-data recall of that same DBLP record; the risk of such contamination—benchmark entries appearing in a model’s training corpus—grows with capability, as stronger models train on larger, newer corpora (Rank et al., 2026).

Two controls, a recall probe and a third-provider late-cutoff model, DeepSeek-V4-Pro, add nuance but do not eliminate the memorization reading; with two models from one provider and a single third-party control, it remains a preliminary signal (§ F.4).

4.5 Stage-2 diagnosis cascade

We compose bibtex-updater (Stage 1) with each of Claude Sonnet 4.6, GPT-5.1 and GPT-5.4 (Stage 2; up to five tool calls per entry) into a cascade. Stage 1 emits verified, a typed hallucinated verdict, or uncertain; only the uncertain entries are forwarded to Stage 2. Since all cascade results use bibtex-updater, the co-design caveat applies (§ G.2). If we treat the entries that neither of the two stages resolves as hallucinated, then on dev_public the Sonnet 4.6 and GPT-5.4 cascades both reach DR 0.9900.990, at FPR 0.0370.037 and 0.0390.039 (Tab. 1); the test_public and stress_test results, and the full panel are in § D.1. The two-stage cascade can therefore be considered a constructive resolution of the false-positive inflation behind failure mode (i).

5 Discussion

Limitations.

Hallmark scores verifiers separately on 14 hallucination types, 6 sub-tests and 3 difficulty tiers, but our analysis has limitations, ordered here by potential influence (full discussion in Appx. I). Because bibtex-updater was co-designed with the taxonomy, it and the cascades built on it should be read as an upper bound on performance (§ G.2), and the FPR-driven deployment bottleneck assumes a venue audit limited by reviewer time (§ 4.4). Most hallucinated entries are synthetic perturbations, and the 108 real-world entries are type-skewed and rated by an automated (LLM) proxy (§ H.6). The core splits are English BibTeX from five ML venues, 2021–2023, supplemented by evaluation-only splits with post-cutoff papers, biomedical and non-ML CS venues, and ChatGPT citations on 42 topics (§ A.3). The post-cutoff resistance of the two latest-cutoff models is descriptive, since recency, provider and contamination are confounded (§ F.4), and hosted-LLM rows are dated snapshots, susceptible to endpoint drift (Tab. 29). Extended-thinking variants were only tested on 100 entries, where larger budgets did not improve F1 once outputs stopped being truncated (§ F.5), and HaRC and verify-citations are excluded because rate limits and blocked lookups keep either from returning its own verdicts at benchmark scale (§ B.2.2). Rankings also depend on the definition of a hallucination, which is set outside the benchmark: counting flags on the four types that cite a real work with wrong details as false accusations puts bibtex-updater ahead of the cascade (§ H.1).

Conclusion.

Despite these limitations, Hallmark gives citation verifiers a shared test and one protocol that separates three failure modes (Tab. 20), which helps venues and individual authors decide whether to deploy them. Our experiments suggest that careful design is required to avoid brittleness caused by, e.g., post-cutoff papers or agentic lookups. The two-stage cascade (§ 4.5) points to a promising direction; since its first stage is our co-designed tool, testing the design with other first-stage verifiers is left for future work. Finally, Hallmark raises a foundational question for the research community: what counts as a hallucinated citation?

AI use statement

Generative-AI tools were used in this work as follows. Among the tasks for which disclosure is required, LLMs generated part of the synthetic data set, namely a subset of the hallucinated entries (controlled plausible fabrications and chimeric titles) generated with GPT-5.1, plus ten plausible_fabrication entries generated with GPT-4o-mini, described in § 3.2 (prompts in § B.2.3), and served as the three automated raters of the reliability proxy in § H.6. Anthropic Claude models—the Opus, Sonnet and Fable families—were used as a coding assistant throughout the implementation of the evaluation harness, the baseline wrappers and bibtex-updater, and assisted in interpreting results and in auditing the paper’s claims and reported numbers against the released artifacts. No LLM formulated the research questions. The taxonomy and the evaluation protocol were conceived by the authors, including the held-out and stress-test splits; LLMs assisted in instantiating them, turning the authors’ taxonomy into concrete type definitions and implementing the protocol. Among the tasks for which disclosure is recommended, the same models assisted with drafting and editing paper sections, with figure-generation code, with literature search, and with reference formatting. Every LLM output that entered the paper, the data, or the code was reviewed by the authors: LLM-generated entries were filtered against bibliographic databases and corrected by the systematic ground-truth audit of § A.3, and reported numbers were recomputed from the released per-entry artifacts. The authors take full responsibility for the content of this paper.

Ethics statement

Hallmark supports scientific integrity by enabling systematic comparison of citation-verification tools, informing venue deployment as LLM-assisted writing becomes standard. A taxonomy of hallucination types could theoretically aid adversaries, but the defensive value of understanding these types outweighs the risk; the taxonomy is derived from publicly documented incidents, not novel attack research. Hallmark is open-source (MIT), GPU-free, and publicly available at https://github.com/rpatrik96/hallmark, ensuring access regardless of institutional resources. The benchmark contains bibliographic metadata only, which is already public: it holds no personal data beyond author names as they appear in published records, and its real-world hallucinated entries come from audits that are themselves public. A flag from any verifier is an accusation against a named author, and at the prevalence of real submissions most flags are false alarms (§ 5); we therefore recommend verifier output as a prompt for human review rather than as a finding, and the released tool routes single-source absence to review instead of flagging it.

Reproducibility statement

Dataset construction, the hallucination taxonomy, and the split definitions are described in § 3.2 and Appx. A. The baseline roster, prompts, model IDs, training cutoffs, decoding parameters, and the agentic tool suite are itemized in § 4.2, § B.2, and § B.2.4; the metric definitions are in § 4.1 and § B.1, and the bootstrap and power-analysis protocol in § B.1. The benchmark and the evaluation harness are released under the MIT license at https://github.com/rpatrik96/hallmark, together with per-tool aggregate results. Per-entry predictions are released for the ablations, for every zero-shot LLM row of the main table, and for bibtex-updater; DOI-only is summary-only, so its aggregates are re-derivable only by re-running the tool. Three of the 42 released result files carry the SHA-256 of the split they scored and a run timestamp; the rest predate that convention and none records a tool version, so a freshness check reports them as unverifiable rather than as fresh. The coverage field in the released aggregates is unreliable—14 of them record 1.01.0 beside a non-zero num_uncertain (worst: llm_openrouter_deepseek_r1_test_public, 180 uncertain, true coverage 0.7830.783)—so the Cov. column of Tab. 1 is read from results/ablations/coverage_reporting.json instead (for bibtex-updater, from coverage.json beside its rescored per-entry verdicts). Most model slugs are floating aliases rather than dated-pinned IDs and the third-party inference endpoints have drifted since collection, so the LLM runs reproduce as dated snapshots rather than as absolute re-runs; § 5 and § B.1 state which results this affects.

Appendix roadmap. The appendix follows the paper’s three failure modes. Each failure mode then has a dedicated home: agentic aggregation (mode i) in Appx. D, base-rate precision and deployment (mode ii) in § E.1, and temporal fragility with its calibration controls (mode iii) in Appx. F. Appendix A Dataset and taxonomy

A.1 Full taxonomy details

Each hallucination type has a characteristic failure signature (Tab. 2), enabling diagnostic analysis of why a tool succeeds or fails.

What is a hallucination?

The question seems almost trivial. But looking into the details exposes a lot of nuance: telling what is not a hallucination is easy (a bit-by-bit match with a trusted database entry), but the reverse is not. Different spellings, handling of diacritics, name conventions (e.g., how Asian names get represented in Latin alphabets), hyphenation rules, and changing author lists across (preprint) versions complicate the picture and do not afford a clear-cut decision. With these caveats in mind, the main goal of Hallmark is to analyze potential failure modes without being too pedantic about unconditionally enforcing bit-by-bit matches where humans can also err, even with the best of intentions. This does not mean tool designers should not strive for perfection, but they need to acknowledge these nuances—especially the ones that have a large effect on deployment.

Verification decision tree.

The tiers reflect a natural workflow: Tier 1 requires single-field lookups (DOI resolution, venue existence); Tier 2 requires cross-referencing (do authors match the resolved DOI record?); Tier 3 demands semantic reasoning (the title almost matches a real paper). A tool that only performs DOI lookups catches Tier 1 but misses Tier 2–3 entirely.

Worked example.

An illustrative near_miss_title pair (Tier 3)—a real entry and its perturbed counterpart, all other fields unchanged:

⬇
title = {Attention is All you Need} % real (Vaswani et al., 2017)
title = {Attention is All you Require} % near_miss_title

The perturbed entry passes the D (DOI), A (authors), V (venue), and F (fields) sub-tests; only T (title exists) and X (cross-DB agreement) fail (Tab. 2), so a DOI-only lookup accepts it, and only title-aware verification catches it.

The taxonomy spans 14 hallucination types across three lookup-difficulty tiers, ordered by the verification effort each type demands. Tier 1 types are settled by one check, either a local field test (year bounds, placeholder strings) or a single lookup (DOI resolution, venue existence). Tier 2 types require cross-referencing two or more resolved fields against each other (authors against the identified paper, venue against the resolved record, preprint against published version). Tier 3 types require multi-source verification or near-duplicate disambiguation (title near-misses, fully plausible fabrications). Three types (merged_citation, partial_author_list, arxiv_version_mismatch) are theoretically motivated compound failure modes: they keep their difficulty tier—2, 2, and 3 respectively—and appear in every core split, with the stress_test split adding depth on them (§ A.3).

A.2 Real-world incident mapping

We mapped 72 real-world hallucinated citations from three documented incident studies to our taxonomy. Tab. 4 shows the mapping results.

Most real-world citations map to a single taxonomy type: of the 72 in this table, 57 (79%) map directly, while the remaining 15 exhibit compound failure modes and take their highest-tier applicable type. The benchmark contains 108 real-world entries in total across all splits; this table covers the 72 drawn from three documented incident studies, and the remaining 36 come from additional documented incidents. plausible_fabrication dominates (55%), reflecting the predominant LLM failure mode: models generate coherent but entirely fictional references rather than subtly corrupting real ones. Three taxonomy types—merged_citation, partial_author_list, and arxiv_version_mismatch—have zero real-world instances, which motivates their designation as stress-test types (§ 3.1).

A.3 Construction details

DBLP scraping.

Valid entries were scraped from the DBLP API (dblp.org/search/publ/api) using venue-specific queries for NeurIPS, ICML, ICLR, AAAI, and CVPR. We retrieved BibTeX records, verified DOI resolution via CrossRef, and confirmed title existence in Semantic Scholar. Entries failing any verification step were excluded.

Perturbation pipeline.

Systematic perturbations follow deterministic rules per hallucination type:

  • •

    fabricated_doi: Replace DOI with a non-resolving DOI using one of 20 non-existent prefixes and four suffix styles (path, identifier, year-indexed, and conference-indexed) to avoid template-detectable patterns.

  • •

    nonexistent_venue: Replace venue with an LLM-generated plausible but nonexistent conference name.

  • •

    placeholder_authors: Replace author list with common placeholder names.

  • •

    future_date: Set year to current year + 5.

  • •

    chimeric_title: Keep authors from paper A, replace title with LLM-generated plausible title.

  • •

    wrong_venue: Keep all fields but swap venue with a different real venue.

  • •

    swapped_authors: Keep title and venue, replace authors with those from a different paper.

  • •

    preprint_as_published: Take an arXiv-only paper and add a fabricated venue field.

  • •

    hybrid_fabrication: Keep a valid DOI but replace title and authors with fabricated metadata.

  • •

    near_miss_title: Modify 1–2 words via six strategies: synonym substitution (POS-safe pairs), plural/singular flipping, British/American spelling swap, abbreviation expansion/contraction (e.g., “RL” ↔\leftrightarrow “Reinforcement Learning”), hyphenation toggling (e.g., “self-supervised” ↔\leftrightarrow “self supervised”), and article removal.

  • •

    plausible_fabrication: Template-based combinatorial generation of a complete, realistic but nonexistent entry (random author combinations, plausible titles, real venues). A separate set of 113 LLM-generated entries (Tab. 15) resembles what an LLM actually emits, but is generated a different way.

  • •

    merged_citation: Combine metadata from 2–3 real papers into one entry (e.g., authors from paper A, title from paper B, venue from paper C).

  • •

    partial_author_list: Take a real paper and drop one or more middle co-authors, keeping only the first and last.

  • •

    arxiv_version_mismatch: Cite an arXiv preprint with a reassigned venue and shifted publication year. Classified as a stress-test type since no real-world instances have been observed.

LLM-generated entries.

We prompted GPT-5.1 to generate plausible but fictional citations for types requiring coherent fabrication (plausible_fabrication, chimeric_title, fabricated_doi). Each prompt requested a BibTeX entry with realistic metadata for a specified ML venue and year range. Generated entries were verified against CrossRef and DBLP: entries with title similarity ≥85%\geq 85\% (token-sort ratio) and author Jaccard similarity ≥0.5\geq 0.5 to any real paper were flagged as potential duplicates of real work and excluded. This filtering removed approximately 12% of generated entries, documenting an LLM recall failure rate where the model reproduces real papers rather than fabricating new ones. The remaining entries were assigned sub-test labels based on their hallucination type’s expected failure pattern.

Real-world collection.

We harvested 72 hallucinated citations from three documented incident studies: GPTZero’s NeurIPS 2025 analysis, GhostCite (Xu et al., 2026), and HalluCitation (Sakai et al., 2026a). Each entry was mapped to the closest taxonomy type based on its failure mode (e.g., a citation with a non-resolving DOI was classified as fabricated_doi; a citation to a non-existent paper with plausible metadata was classified as plausible_fabrication). The real-world sample is type-skewed: 55% are plausible_fabrication, reflecting the predominant LLM failure mode in practice. Types without real-world examples (merged_citation, partial_author_list, arxiv_version_mismatch) appear in every core split alongside the 11 empirical types; the stress_test split adds evaluation depth on them (§ 3.1).

Adversarial crafting.

We manually constructed entries designed to evade specific detection strategies. These include entries with DOIs that resolve to unrelated papers (hybrid_fabrication), entries combining metadata from multiple real papers (merged_citation), and entries with plausible but non-existent venues chosen to be close to real venue names. Adversarial entries stress-test tool robustness beyond what template-based perturbation achieves.

Quality control.

Every generated entry passes through automated validation: (1) BibTeX well-formedness check (valid syntax, and the required fields for the entry’s own type: author/title/journal/year for @article, booktitle for @inproceedings, publisher for @book, school for theses, institution for @techreport, and author/title/year for @misc, with journal waived for an @article carrying an arXiv identifier), (2) sub-test label consistency (sub-test ground truth matches the hallucination type’s expected failure pattern), (3) cross-validation with the valid entry pool to prevent accidental duplicates.

Extension splits.

Four evaluation-only splits are released alongside the main splits, outside the dev/test/hidden partition (Tab. 5). The temporal probe (60 entries: 30 valid / 30 hallucinated) is the small pre-supplement probe of post-cutoff behavior. Its valid half pairs 15 papers from 2024 with 15 from 2026, the latter scraped from arXiv ML categories via the arXiv API (scripts/probe_temporal_robustness.py); its hallucinated half (18 from 2024, 12 from 2026) combines 21 perturbation and 9 adversarial entries. The 448-entry temporal supplement (§ F.1) validates the probe’s findings at scale; the probe additionally covers 2026 arXiv submissions. The cross-domain split (test_crossdomain, 500 entries: 200 valid / 300 hallucinated) probes transfer outside the ML-venue regime the main splits sample: 299 biomedical entries (156 PubMed, 143 bioRxiv) and 201 from non-ML CS venues (OSDI, CCS, CHI, USENIX Security, KDD, SIGGRAPH, and others). Valid entries are scraped; hallucinated entries follow the perturbation pipeline across the taxonomy, including the stress types, with 80/140/80 entries in Tiers 1/2/3; pre-screening uses reference_year 2026 for this split. bibtex-updater’s evaluation on this split is in § G.2. The ChatGPT-citation supplement (341 entries: 172 valid / 169 hallucinated) converts the hand-coded corpus of Walters & Wilder (2023) into authentic, multidisciplinary ChatGPT hallucinations; its construction and results are in § C.6.

The three sources play complementary roles: perturbation entries are controlled diagnostic tests that isolate specific verification capabilities, while LLM-generated entries look like the hallucinations that occur in practice and real-world entries are documented to have occurred; stratifying by generation method lets us assess each independently.

Base-paper overlap across splits.

Perturbation entries keep the fields they do not corrupt, so a hallucinated entry can be traced to its base paper by DOI or normalized title. On the public partition the bases are disjoint: 0 of 606 dev_public hallucinated entries match a test_public valid entry, 0 of 519 the other way, the two valid pools share no entry, and two base papers are perturbed in both splits. The auxiliary splits are not disjoint from the public pools: 109 of 244 test_hidden hallucinated entries match a valid entry in dev_public (70) or test_public (39), three test_hidden valid entries duplicate dev_public ones, and 109 of 121 stress_test entries match a valid entry in test_public (64), test_hidden (46), or dev_public (8). Results on test_hidden and stress_test therefore measure robustness to new perturbations of partly seen base papers, not to unseen papers; the public dev/test comparison is the base-paper-disjoint one.

Quality control and design choices.

Every entry undergoes automated validation (field completeness, BibTeX well-formedness, sub-test consistency); see § A.3 for the validation rules and acceptance criteria.

We blind the url field at dispatch, so a verifier never sees it and cannot substitute URL resolution for citation verification. The released corpus still stores the field—114 of the 1,950 public entries and 453 of the 454 test_hidden entries carry one—because blinding was applied when an entry was handed to a tool rather than when it was written. One ad-hoc resume runner read the corpus files directly and skipped that step, so a few checkpoints did ship the field into the prompt. The released prediction records make the exposure measurable: the worst-affected main-table row exposes 7 entries of 1,119, which bounds the shift at under one percentage point of FPR even if every exposed verdict flipped. Blinding is now enforced when an entry is constructed rather than at each dispatch site. We include canary strings for contamination detection (unique fixed tokens embedded in dataset metadata; if a model outputs them verbatim, it has memorized the split). No evaluated model emitted a canary token in any released prediction record. We use uniform type distribution to maximize per-type power; reweighting utilities support prevalence-adjusted evaluation. The API supports generation-method stratification for assessing tool performance on perturbation vs. LLM-generated vs. real-world entries.

What we transfer from HumanEval (Chen et al., 2021) is the unit-test-per-instance structure rather than its execution semantics. HumanEval ships every problem with its own assertion suite, so a failing candidate names the property it violated instead of merely lowering a scalar; Hallmark ships every entry with its own six declared sub-test outcomes, so a verifier’s error localizes to the verification property it missed. The analogy stops at execution: our sub-tests are metadata checks with declared expected values, not code run against hidden inputs, so there is no pass@kk analog and no partial credit within an entry. We use uniform type distribution to maximize per-type power; reweighting utilities support prevalence-adjusted evaluation. The API supports generation-method stratification for assessing tool performance on perturbation vs. LLM-generated vs. real-world entries.

A.4 Datasheet for Hallmark

Following Gebru et al. (2021) and Holland et al. (2020), we provide a datasheet for the Hallmark dataset.

Motivation.

Hallmark was created to provide a standardized benchmark for evaluating citation hallucination detection tools, motivated by the NeurIPS 2025 incident and subsequent audits.

Composition.

The public release contains 2,072 BibTeX entries: 826 valid entries scraped from DBLP and arXiv and 1,246 hallucinated entries generated through perturbation, LLM generation, adversarial crafting, and real-world collection across 14 hallucination types. A held-out test_hidden split contains 454 additional entries (210 valid, 244 hallucinated, for 1,036 valid entries in total) (per-entry labels withheld; aggregate label counts in Tab. 5), bringing the grand total to 2,526. Split counts: dev_public 1,119 (513 valid / 606 hallucinated), test_public 831 (312 / 519), stress_test 122 (1 / 121). The dev/test/hidden split is deterministic: stratified by hallucination type and tier with seed=8042 (recorded in metadata.json), so the partition is regenerable from the released corpus. Each entry includes 6 binary sub-test labels. Four evaluation-only splits are released alongside the 2,526-entry benchmark, outside the dev/test/hidden partition: a 60-entry temporal probe, a 448-entry temporal supplement (2024–2025), a 500-entry cross-domain split, and a 341-entry supplement of authentic ChatGPT-generated citations converted from Walters & Wilder (2023) (Tab. 5; the ChatGPT supplement’s construction in § C.6).

Collection process.

Valid entries were scraped from the DBLP API and verified against CrossRef and Semantic Scholar. Hallucinated entries were generated using the methods described in § 3.2 and § A.3.

Preprocessing/Cleaning/Labeling.

BibTeX records were normalized to a consistent field ordering. Unicode characters were preserved. Entries were split into dev/test/hidden sets by stratified sampling across hallucination types and tiers (deterministic seed: see Composition). Labels were assigned deterministically by the generation pipeline; valid entries carry ground-truth sub-test labels derived from database cross-checks. The released corpus is post-relabel: a systematic ground-truth audit (scripts/relabel_ground_truth.py, commits 32fe9d6 and 1475a2f) re-resolved entries against live databases and corrected real papers that had been mislabeled HALLUCINATED; the per-entry flip log is released at results/reviewer_experiments/relabel_flips.json.

Recommended uses.

Hallmark is intended for evaluating and comparing citation verification tools, ablating individual verification sub-tests, and cross-tool ranking via tier-weighted F1 and Plackett-Luce infrastructure.

Non-recommended uses.

Hallmark should not be used to train hallucination generators, to produce convincing fake citations, or for any purpose that violates the MIT license.

Distribution.

The dataset is distributed under the MIT license (https://opensource.org/licenses/MIT) via GitHub at https://github.com/rpatrik96/hallmark. The content release reported throughout this paper is pinned to repository tag v1.2.0, which fixes the byte-level split contents—the core splits are byte-identical to the post-relabel v1.1.1, and v1.2.0 adds the evaluation-only extension artifacts—and a manifest.json carrying sha256 digests pins the precomputed baseline-result files, which tag v1.2.3 moved to data/v1.2/baseline_results/. A Croissant 1.0 metadata record is included in the repository root. The test_hidden split is not publicly distributed.

Maintenance.

The benchmark is maintained by the authors and accepts community contributions through pull requests validated by automated checks for BibTeX well-formedness, sub-test consistency, and duplicate detection. Two version axes are tracked separately. Each entry carries a schema_version field (1.0) recording the record structure; the schema is stable and the data/v1.0/ directory name reflects it. The content release—which corrections update as point releases—is identified by the version field in metadata.json (1.2.0; the ground-truth relabel landed in 1.1.1) and the matching repository tag v1.2.0. The co-designed reference tool bibtex-updater is pinned to git tag v1.2.0 throughout: both the standalone results (§ G.2) and the cascade Stage 1 (Tab. 22). The cascade Stage 2 is a dated snapshot (Sonnet 4.6 via OpenRouter, 2026-09-21), as LLM endpoints drift (§ 5). The released per-entry bibtex-updater verdicts (results/relabel_delta/btu_v1_2_0_prescreen_fix/bibtexupdater_{dev,test}_public_per_entry.jsonl alongside data/v1.0/baseline_results/bibtexupdater_{dev,test}_public.json) let a reader recompute the bibtex-updater aggregates (DR 0.820, FPR 0.051) offline, without re-installing the tool or re-querying external databases. Robustness ablations collected against third-party inference endpoints carry a snapshot date and an endpoint-drift caveat (§ 5), so they are reproducible as dated within-run deltas rather than as absolute re-runs.

Ethical and legal considerations.

Hallmark contains only bibliographic metadata; it includes no personally identifiable information beyond author names already present in published bibliographic records. No human subjects are involved and no IRB approval is required.

Appendix B Evaluation protocol and reproducibility

B.1 Metrics and statistical analysis

The two errors and the summary metrics.

The two trade off against different deployment costs. A missed fabrication that reaches print is usually the worse error—costlier than a false alarm a reviewer can dismiss—but which error dominates depends on the regime: prevalence (the fraction of entries that are hallucinated), the cost ratio cFN/cFPc_{\text{FN}}/c_{\text{FP}}, and reviewer capacity (§ 4.4). We report the false-negative rate =1−DR=1-\text{DR} for completeness.

Four further metrics summarize a tool in a single number. F1-Hallucination is the harmonic mean of precision and recall on the hallucinated class; it is prevalence-sensitive, so we compare it only within a split. TW-F1 weights each hallucinated entry by its tier (1/2/3), rewarding the detection of harder hallucinations; the ranking of the three tools we swept (DOI-only, GPT-5.1, and bibtex-updater) held across uniform, linear, and quadratic weightings in the sweep we ran, which we now report with a caveat on the sweep itself (§ B.1).

Tier-weighted F1.

For entries {ei}\{e_{i}\} with tier weights wi∈{1,2,3}w_{i}\in\{1,2,3\}, predictions y^i\hat{y}_{i}, and labels yiy_{i}:

TW-Precision =∑iwi⋅𝟏[y^i=yi=H]∑iwi⋅𝟏[y^i=H],\displaystyle=\frac{\sum_{i}w_{i}\cdot\mathbf{1}[\hat{y}_{i}=y_{i}=\text{H}]}{\sum_{i}w_{i}\cdot\mathbf{1}[\hat{y}_{i}=\text{H}]}, TW-Recall =∑iwi⋅𝟏[y^i=yi=H]∑iwi⋅𝟏[yi=H],\displaystyle=\frac{\sum_{i}w_{i}\cdot\mathbf{1}[\hat{y}_{i}=y_{i}=\text{H}]}{\sum_{i}w_{i}\cdot\mathbf{1}[y_{i}=\text{H}]}, (1)

where H denotes the hallucinated class, and TW-F1 is their harmonic mean. Valid entries carry no difficulty tier, so false positives contribute uniform weight 1.0 in the TW-Precision denominator. Because false positives carry uniform weight while true positives are tier-weighted, TW-F1 can be inflated by aggressive over-flagging; MCC provides a complementary prevalence-corrected view.

Expected Calibration Error.

We partition predictions into B=10B=10 equal-width confidence bins and compute:

ECE=∑b=1B|Sb|N​|acc​(Sb)−conf​(Sb)|,\text{ECE}=\sum_{b=1}^{B}\frac{|S_{b}|}{N}\left|\text{acc}(S_{b})-\text{conf}(S_{b})\right|, (2)

where SbS_{b} is the set of predictions in bin bb, acc​(Sb)\text{acc}(S_{b}) is the fraction of correct predictions, and conf​(Sb)\text{conf}(S_{b}) is the mean confidence. Adaptive (equal-mass) binning is available in the codebase.

Baseline integration.

Hallmark provides a baseline registry that supports discovery, availability checking, and dispatch for all integrated tools. New baselines register via a decorator pattern, specifying their dependencies and whether they require API keys. A weekly CI workflow re-runs the DOI-only baseline in full and a 50-entry stratified verify-citations sample on the dev split, and validates the pre-computed rate-limited baselines by checksum. The stress_test split contains 122 entries: 121 hallucinated plus a single valid canary entry planted for contamination detection; with one valid entry FPR is not meaningful, so we report only Detection Rate. Read that rate with the split’s composition in mind: 75 of the 122 entries (61.5%61.5\%) are partial_author_list or arxiv_version_mismatch, both of which describe a real work inaccurately, and every one of the cascade’s misses on this split falls in that class.

The statistical procedures below underlie every numerical claim in the paper. Bootstrap CIs accompany the aggregate metrics in Tab. 1 and the per-type breakdown in Tab. 13; paired bootstrap pp-values support pairwise tool comparisons in § 4.3; the per-type power analysis (Tab. 6) bounds which type-level differences in Tab. 13 are statistically distinguishable.

Bootstrap confidence intervals.
Scoring conventions for Tab. 1.

Small gaps are point-estimate orderings—rankings by the single measured value, with no test that the gap is statistically real: the Sonnet 4.6 / Opus 4.7 F1 gap of 0.3 pp on dev_public is not significant (paired bootstrap on the 2026-09-02 per-entry verdicts, 10,000 resamples: 95% CI on the difference [−1.5,+2.2][-1.5,+2.2] pp, two-sided p=0.74p{=}0.74; § B.1). Abstentions—entries a tool declines to label either way—are handled differently by the two blocks, and the difference favors the abstaining LLMs. An uncertain verdict from an LLM verifier is excluded from the DR/FPR/F1 triple, so those rates are computed over the entries the model committed to; bibtex-updater resolves its own abstentions to valid before scoring, so they count against its DR. DeepSeek-R1 shows the size of the gap: 21.7%21.7\% of its test_public verdicts are uncertain—in its case API error fallbacks rather than deliberate abstentions (Tab. 9)—and excluding them puts its DR at 0.8090.809 where the committed-valid convention would give 0.6440.644. Coverage and an aggressive re-flagging stance are in § E.2; the Cov. column of Tab. 1 is read from results/ablations/coverage_reporting.json, because the released aggregates record coverage 1.01.0 in 14 of 42 files that also report a non-zero num_uncertain and so cannot reproduce it. Predictions were collected 2026-05-05, except the Sonnet 4.6 and Opus 4.7 rows of Tab. 1 (2026-09-02, marked §); hosted-LLM rows are dated snapshots subject to endpoint drift (§ 5).

The aggregate metrics in Tab. 1 are accompanied by 95% confidence intervals computed via stratified bootstrap with 10,000 resamples (seed=42), wherever a tool’s full-coverage per-entry predictions are available. Stratification by hallucination type ensures that the resampled datasets preserve the original type distribution, preventing bootstrap bias from underrepresented types. For reference, GPT-5.1’s dev_public 95% CIs are: DR [0.812, 0.861]; F1 [0.747, 0.785] (point estimates 0.837 / 0.766). The released result files carry Wilson intervals on the per-type detection rates; their aggregate *_ci fields are null, so the bootstrap intervals quoted in this paper are not recoverable from the release and would have to be recomputed from the per-entry dumps. DOI-only is summary-only on dev_public—its released aggregates were reconstructed from confusion-matrix counts rather than stored per-entry predictions—so we report its point estimate without a CI or a paired test on that split. bibtex-updater’s full-coverage per-entry verdicts are released on both splits and recompute its point estimates exactly; as a co-designed tool it is reported separately from the independent-tool comparison (Tab. 36), so we give its point estimates without a paired bootstrap.

Significance testing.

We use paired bootstrap tests (Efron & Tibshirani, 1994) to compare tools pairwise. For each pair of tools (A,B)(A,B), we resample entries with replacement and compute Δ=F1A−F1B\Delta=\text{F1}_{A}-\text{F1}_{B} for each resample. The two-sided pp-value is min⁡(1, 2⋅min⁡(P⁡(Δ≤0),P⁡(Δ≥0)))\min\!\left(1,\,2\cdot\min\!\left(P(\Delta\leq 0),\,P(\Delta\geq 0)\right)\right); taking 2⋅P⁡(Δ≤0)2\cdot P(\Delta\leq 0) alone returns p=1p=1 whenever the first-named tool is the weaker one. The only headline pair we test is Sonnet 4.6 vs. Opus 4.7. On dev_public their F1 gap (++0.003) is not significant (CI [−0.015,+0.022][-0.015,+0.022], two-sided p=0.74p{=}0.74); on test_public: Sonnet’s F1 (0.907, CI [0.891, 0.923]) exceeds Opus’s (0.889, CI [0.872, 0.906]) by ++0.018, one-sided p=0.023p{=}0.023, two-sided p=0.045p{=}0.045, Cohen’s h=0.059h{=}0.059: borderline-significant at α=0.05\alpha{=}0.05 with a negligible effect size. The bootstrap confidence interval on the difference, [+0.001,+0.035][+0.001,+0.035], excludes zero by a margin narrower than the endpoint drift between collections (Tab. 29), and on the earlier collection the sign of this gap is reversed, so we do not read it as establishing an ordering between the two models. The bibtex-updater-vs-Sonnet F1 comparison sits across the co-design boundary, so we report it as a point-estimate difference without a paired pp-value.

Per-type power analysis.

Per-type counts cap the resolution of type-level comparisons. On dev_public they run from 26 (hybrid_fabrication) to 76 (plausible_fabrication) with a median of 41, and on test_public from 23 to 66; the smallest buckets are those from which the ground-truth audit reassigned real papers (see Tab. 5 caption). For detection rate, a type with 30 hallucinated entries and 90% true detection rate has a 95% Clopper-Pearson confidence interval of [0.74,0.98][0.74,0.98], compared to [0.55,0.998][0.55,0.998] at n=10n=10.

Type-level power is modest, so only large per-type gaps are detectable. Tab. 6 reports the minimum detectable effect (Minimum Detectable Effect (MDE)) at 80% power (α=0.05\alpha=0.05, two-sided zz-test) for each hallucination type in the dev_public split. A type with n=30n=30 has an MDE of 25.6pp for a single tool; for the difference between two tools it is about 36pp in the worst case (about 22pp for plausible_fabrication, n=76n=76), so smaller per-type gaps between tools are not reliably detected. These values bound which per-type comparisons are statistically meaningful.

Tier weight sensitivity.

We evaluate tier-weighted F1 under five weighting schemes: uniform {1,1,1}\{1,1,1\} (equivalent to unweighted F1), linear {1,2,3}\{1,2,3\} (default), quadratic {1,4,9}\{1,4,9\}, log {log⁡(2),log⁡(3),log⁡(4)}\{\log(2),\log(3),\log(4)\}, and inverse difficulty (weights proportional to 1−mean DR1-\text{mean DR} across tools). Tab. 7 reports TW-F1 for the three reference tools across all five schemes.

The bibtex-updater column has been re-run on the rescored predictions; the other two have not, and two caveats bound how much they show. First, the implementation that produced Tab. 7 read the false-positive rate under a key the emitter does not write, so it defaulted on every call and the quantity actually swept was tier-weighted recall: the sweep could not see a false positive. The lookup is fixed in the released harness but the sweep has not been re-run, and no sensitivity artifact is in the release, so read this table as evidence that the recall ordering is weight-insensitive and not as evidence about TW-F1 as we define it. Second, the DOI-only column predates the resolver correction of § B.2: its linear cell reads 0.3100.310 where the current run reports TW-F1 0.2680.268 (Tab. 1). Weight-insensitivity is in any case the weaker of the two robustness questions: the ordering does not survive a change in what counts as a hallucination (§ H.1). bibtex-updater’s narrow post-relabel sensitivity range (0.880–0.901) reflects its consistently strong per-tier performance; DOI-only shows wider variation (0.255–0.392) because its detection is concentrated in Tier 1.

B.2 Evaluation implementation

All baselines are implemented as Python wrappers conforming to the Hallmark baseline interface. Each wrapper: (1) converts Hallmark BenchmarkEntry objects to the tool’s expected input format, (2) invokes the tool, (3) maps the tool’s output to a Hallmark Prediction with label, confidence, and reason (Fig. 4).

B.2.1 Pre-screening layer specification

The pre-screening layer implements four checks that run before external tool invocation:

  1. 1.

    DOI resolution: Normalizes the DOI (strips a URL prefix and, for arXiv DOIs, a version suffix such as v1, since DataCite registers only the unversioned form) and sends a live HTTP HEAD request to doi.org. Only a 404 or 410 served by doi.org itself flags the entry; a missing or malformed DOI, a network error, a rate limit, a block or a server error yields no verdict, so a transient failure never overrides the tool.

  2. 2.

    Year bounds checking: Flags entries with publication years in the future or before 1900.11 1 Genuinely valid pre-1900 references exist, of course (classical mathematics and physics citations); the bound is a corpus-tuned heuristic—no entry pool in the benchmark carries a publication year before 2021—so deployments verifying older literature should relax or drop this check.

  3. 3.

    Author name heuristics: Detects common placeholder patterns (“John Doe,” “A. Author,” single-word author names, repeated names).

  4. 4.

    Capitalized-token placeholders: Flags author fields built from placeholder tokens that the previous check misses: a capitalized word followed by digits (Smith2), a field made only of initials, or one where more than half the tokens are all-uppercase words.

Pre-screening results are tagged with [Pre-screening override] in the reason string to maintain transparency about which detections come from the pre-screening layer vs. the external tool.

B.2.2 HaRC and verify-citations: why neither is in the main table

We attempted HaRC (HaRC Contributors, 2024) and verify-citations (verify-citations Contributors, 2025) as full-coverage baselines and could not obtain a verdict from either at benchmark scale. The binding constraint for HaRC is not Semantic Scholar throttling but harcx’s own lookup path, which queries Google Scholar through scholarly: Scholar blocks the client, the library retries rather than failing, and under the -q --threshold 0.75 invocation our wrapper uses even a single-entry .bib does not complete within 150 s. Dropping -q returns in seconds but emits no verdict line at all, exit 0. An authenticated S2 key (1 RPS, 5-hour budget) does not change either behavior, so 0 of 1,119 entries are actually checked by harcx. verify-citations exhibits the same throughput pathology and we never ran it over a full split; the released artifact for it covers a 500-entry sample. In both cases whatever verdicts a run does produce come from the shared pre-screening layer (§ B.2.1) rather than from the tool, so the numbers would not measure what the row claims to measure.

Both tools are therefore excluded from Tab. 1. The one keyed HaRC artifact we release (harc_with_s2key_dev_public.json) records DR = 0.209, FPR = 0.045, F1 = 0.335 over all 1,119 entries, but every one of those verdicts is a pre-screening verdict, and the file is scored against the pre-relabel ground truth (633 hallucinated / 486 valid, against the current 606/513), so it is comparable to no other number in this paper and we register it as known-stale rather than report it as a baseline.

B.2.3 Baseline wrappers and prompt template
LLM prompt template.

The LLM-based baselines (GPT-5.1, Claude, and OpenRouter models) use a zero-shot prompt with no few-shot examples. The exact template, reproduced verbatim from hallmark/baselines/llm_verifier.py (VERIFICATION_PROMPT; {bibtex} is the substituted entry), is:

⬇
You are a citation verification expert. Analyze the following BibTeX entry and determine if it is a VALID real publication or a HALLUCINATED (fabricated) citation.
BibTeX entry:
‘‘‘bibtex
{bibtex}
‘‘‘
Consider:
1. Is the title plausible and does it match known work by these authors?
2. Are the authors real researchers in this field?
3. Is the venue (journal/conference) real?
4. Does the year make sense?
5. If a DOI is present, does it look properly formatted?
When the entry is HALLUCINATED, classify the hallucination mode using exactly one of:
‘fabricated_doi‘, ‘nonexistent_venue‘, ‘placeholder_authors‘, ‘future_date‘,
‘chimeric_title‘, ‘wrong_venue‘, ‘swapped_authors‘, ‘preprint_as_published‘,
‘hybrid_fabrication‘, ‘near_miss_title‘, ‘plausible_fabrication‘,
‘merged_citation‘, ‘partial_author_list‘, ‘arxiv_version_mismatch‘.
Brief definitions:
- ‘fabricated_doi‘: DOI does not resolve / is invented.
- ‘nonexistent_venue‘: venue/journal does not exist.
- ‘placeholder_authors‘: authors are placeholders ("Author1", "et al." alone, etc.).
- ‘future_date‘: year is in the future relative to publication.
- ‘chimeric_title‘: title combines fragments from multiple real works.
- ‘wrong_venue‘: real paper but cited at wrong venue.
- ‘swapped_authors‘: authors swapped or mismatched against the real paper.
- ‘preprint_as_published‘: arXiv preprint cited as published in a venue.
- ‘hybrid_fabrication‘: real DOI but other metadata (authors/title) doesn’t match the DOI target.
- ‘near_miss_title‘: title differs from a real paper by small but meaningful edits.
- ‘plausible_fabrication‘: entirely fabricated yet plausible-sounding paper.
- ‘merged_citation‘: metadata combined from two real papers.
- ‘partial_author_list‘: real paper but author list is incomplete.
- ‘arxiv_version_mismatch‘: arXiv version cited as a different version (or as published).
Respond with JSON only:
{
"label": "VALID" or "HALLUCINATED" or "UNCERTAIN",
"confidence": 0.0 to 1.0,
"predicted_hallucination_type": "<one of the 14 types above, or null>",
"reason": "brief explanation"
}
‘predicted_hallucination_type‘ MUST be null when label is VALID or UNCERTAIN.
B.2.4 Reproducibility: LLM experimental setup
Model roster.

The evaluation pipeline accepts any OpenRouter-, OpenAI-, or Anthropic-compatible model ID as a drop-in kwarg (model=...). Tab. 8 lists every zero-shot baseline reported in the paper, the API endpoint used for the predictions in data/v1.0/baseline_results/ and results/temporal_supplement/, and the corresponding training cutoff (cross-referenced against Tab. 27). The two Anthropic models are reachable through both the native API (baselines llm_anthropic and llm_anthropic_opus_4_7) and the OpenRouter mirror; we use the OpenRouter mirror for the released predictions. Agentic baselines (llm_agentic_openai, llm_agentic_btu_openai) use gpt-5.1; the reported Anthropic agentic-bibtex-updater run (llm_agentic_btu_sonnet_4_6) uses the OpenRouter mirror anthropic/claude-sonnet-4.6, matching the zero-shot Sonnet endpoint. The registry also retains legacy native-API agentic variants (llm_agentic_anthropic, llm_agentic_btu_anthropic) hard-coded to claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929; these are not used for any number reported in the paper. OpenRouter is accessed via the OpenAI SDK with base_url=https://openrouter.ai/api/v1. All zero-shot, DOI-only, and bibtex-updater main-run predictions in data/v1.0/baseline_results/ were collected on 2026-05-05 via the endpoints above; hosted-LLM rows are dated snapshots subject to endpoint drift (§ 5).

Decoding configuration.

Zero-shot calls request temperature=0.0 on every endpoint that accepts it. The one forced exception is gpt-5.5, which the code sets to temperature=1.0; gpt-5.1 and gpt-5.4 are sent temperature=0.0, but the GPT-5 endpoint samples stochastically regardless of the requested value (E3 in § F.4 measures the resulting run-to-run variance). The completion-token budget is max_completion_tokens=1024 on OpenAI- and OpenRouter-compatible endpoints—sized to absorb hidden thinking tokens emitted by reasoning models—and max_tokens=256 on the Anthropic native endpoint. This single 1024-(non-Anthropic)/256-(Anthropic-native) split applies to every main-table, temporal-supplement, and cutoff-aware run; the thinking-budget smoke test (§ F.5) deliberately sweeps around this budget to locate the saturation boundary. We pass seed=42 on OpenAI-SDK-compatible endpoints; the Anthropic Messages API does not expose an equivalent. OpenRouter is left on its default dynamic provider routing (no provider pin), so an open-weight slug may be served by different underlying providers (e.g. DeepInfra, Together, Fireworks) on different runs; the OpenRouter rows are therefore reproducible only as dated snapshots. The zero-shot prompt (§ B.2.3) is sent as a single user-role message with no system prompt. We do not use JSON mode; responses are parsed with a tolerant extractor that handles bare JSON and fenced code blocks, with an UNCERTAIN@0.5 fallback on parse failure (throughout, label@cc denotes the label assigned with confidence cc). Agentic calls use a 1024-token completion budget to accommodate tool-call turns. Client-side retry is max_retries=5 for zero-shot and 3 for agentic baselines, with a 120 s per-request timeout.

Agentic baselines: tools and iteration.

We evaluate four agentic variants: OpenAI (gpt-5.1) and Anthropic (OpenRouter anthropic/claude-sonnet-4.6) backends, each with either a multi-source tool suite or bibtex-updater-as-tool. The OpenAI agentic and the Anthropic agentic-bibtex-updater runs are the variants reported in the paper; numbers come from data/v1.0/baseline_results/llm_agentic_btu_sonnet_4_6_dev_public.json and the corresponding OpenAI checkpoint. Tools are exposed via the provider’s native function-calling interface with tool_choice="auto": the model may answer without any tool call, and we track the parametric-vs-tool split per prediction. Up to MAX_TOOL_CALLS=5 invocations per entry, plus one final verdict turn. If the cap is exceeded without a verdict, the entry is assigned UNCERTAIN@0.5.

The multi-source suite comprises 4 tools, each returning {authors, title, venue, year, doi} with fields truncated to 500 characters:

  • •

    resolve_doi(doi): CrossRef DOI resolution (api.crossref.org/works/{doi}).

  • •

    search_crossref(query, limit=5): CrossRef bibliographic search (max 20 results).

  • •

    search_openalex(query, limit=5): OpenAlex polite pool (max 25).

  • •

    search_arxiv(query, limit=5): arXiv Atom API (max 20).

All HTTP requests use a HALLMARK/1.0 User-Agent and 10–15 s timeouts; tool exceptions are retried with exponential backoff (up to 3 retries, base delay 1 s).

The bibtex-updater-as-tool variant exposes a single tool, verify_with_bibtex_updater(bibtex), that invokes the bibtex-check CLI with --rate-limit 120 --academic-only, returning {status, confidence, mismatched_fields, api_sources, errors}. Subprocess timeout: 180 s.

External-database access.

The three database-backed endpoints—DOI-only, standalone bibtex-updater, and the agentic suite—query five external services: CrossRef (api.crossref.org, polite pool, no key), OpenAlex (polite pool, identified by a mailto contact), Semantic Scholar (the graph/v1 paper-lookup API, accessed with an S2_API_KEY), the arXiv Atom API, and DBLP. Semantic Scholar resolves a citation by matching its title, authors, venue, and identifiers against the S2 corpus and returning the canonical record—or none—which is the evidence bibtex-updater weighs to confirm or flag an entry. Semantic Scholar requires an API key for reliable programmatic access: the free key moves requests off the throttled shared public pool onto a dedicated per-key rate limit. The key affects only throughput and reliability: an unauthenticated re-run hits the shared limit (frequent HTTP 429) and resolves the corpus more slowly, but queries the same records and returns the same matches, so it does not change the reported verdicts. The main-run numbers were queried on 2026-05-04/05. Agentic tool results are replayable offline from the released sha256-keyed tool-cache (mechanics under Tool-call caching below), so the agentic baselines reproduce without live calls. The DOI-only and standalone-bibtex-updater endpoints have no such cache, so their numbers are dated snapshots of the corresponding databases.

System prompts.

The multi-source agentic system prompt:

The bibtex-updater-as-tool agentic system prompt:

Tool-call caching.

Agentic tool results are cached in SQLite keyed on sha256(tool_name::canonical_args_json). TTL is disabled by default; cache hits bypass the network. This is a reproducibility artifact, transparent to the LLM.

Failure handling.

After three consecutive API errors, the baseline aborts and marks remaining entries as UNCERTAIN@0.5 with reason tag [Error fallback]. These entries count as abstentions in Cov. and contribute zero to detection rate.

Appendix C Core results and validity

C.1 Full test_public results

Cross-split observations (from the main text).
  • •

    Cross-split FPR shifts vary by model. Most LLMs gain or hold F1 on test_public; FPR shifts range from under 11 pp (GPT-5.4, both Geminis) to about +8+8 pp (the Qwen variants), with Sonnet 4.6 at +2.6+2.6 pp and Opus 4.7 at +5.1+5.1 pp. DeepSeek-R1’s −30.3-30.3 pp is a denominator artifact—180 of its 831 test_public verdicts are API error fallbacks recorded as uncertain—not a precision gain. All shifts sit within bootstrap-CI width at nvalid=312n_{\text{valid}}{=}312.

  • •

    bibtex-updater is cross-split stable. Its FPR rises only +2.9+2.9 pp (0.051→0.0800.051{\to}0.080) and DR and F1 hold: conservative matching flags so sparingly that test_public’s harder valid pool does not inflate its false positives, and its flat risk–coverage curve—the error rate as a function of the fraction of entries it commits to, traced by varying the abstention threshold—confirms the low FPR is structural, arising from conservative matching rather than from abstention (a reading the coverage re-scoring puts in question; § E.2).

  • •

    Both agentic bibtex-updater harnesses lose part of their dev-side FPR inflation on test_public. Sonnet+bibtex-updater FPR drops −8.8-8.8 pp and GPT-5.1+bibtex-updater −11.4-11.4 pp cross-split, shrinking each harness’s dev-side multiplier, but the harness-driven precision cost persists in both.

Tab. 9 reports all tools with both dev_public and test_public evaluations: the DOI-only baseline, twelve zero-shot LLM verifiers, three agentic harnesses, bibtex-updater, and the always-call evidence-injection co-designed variant.

C.2 LLM baseline agreement and calibration
