Appendix F Failure mode (iii): temporal fragility and calibration

Following LiveCodeBench (Jain et al., 2025), we tag entries with three temporal segments (pre-2023, 2023–2024, 2025+) so the benchmark can measure how verifiers degrade on recent papers (§ 4.4). We read that degradation through the cross-regime ranking, which is prompt-invariant, rather than through absolute post-cutoff FPR, which a prompt-sensitivity sweep moves by 1010–3737 percentage points (pp) on wording alone (§ H.2).

Training-data cutoffs of evaluated LLMs.

The temporal evaluation assumes papers from calendar years 2024–2025 post-date most evaluated models’ training data. Tab. 27 compiles vendor-disclosed training cutoffs (or the most recent reliable upper bound when no disclosure is available) for every LLM used as a baseline. Three observations frame the temporal results. (i) Every evaluated model has a disclosed or inferred cutoff no later than late 2025, so the 448-entry temporal supplement (drawn from 2024–2025 DBLP proceedings) is partially or fully out-of-distribution for all of them. (ii) The two closed-weight models with earliest cutoffs (GPT-5.1, Sep 2024) and the conservative open-weight Gemini 2.5 Flash (Jan 2025) are hardest-hit by the post-cutoff FPR rise, consistent with their reliance on parametric confirmation. (iii) DeepSeek models do not publish an official cutoff in their technical reports, so we report the OpenRouter-surfaced metadata and flag it as a provenance gap that future versions of Hallmark should track via release-date probes.

2024–2025 DBLP papers are out-of-distribution to varying degrees across the cohort: late-2025 entries are post-cutoff for every model, while early-2024 entries are post-cutoff only for the earliest-cutoff models (GPT-5.1: Sep 2024; DeepSeek-R1: Jul 2024). Across the nine non-Anthropic LLMs tested on the supplement the temporal hit splits into four regimes: four models with healthy baselines degrade sharply (GPT-5.1, Gemini 2.5 Flash, Mistral Large, Llama 4 Maverick; Δ\DeltaFPR  ++35–62 pp); three with already-elevated baselines stay near-ceiling or worsen (Qwen3-235B, DeepSeek-V3.2, Qwen3-VL-235B at FPR 0.89, a new cohort maximum); DeepSeek-R1’s run failed on 151 of the 448 entries, leaving only its FPR of 0.856 evaluable (Tab. 28, footnote †\dagger); and Gemini 2.5 Pro over-flags only moderately (FPR 0.25). Pro-tier post-training, not data recency, drives that last case: Gemini 2.5 Flash—same vendor, comparable cutoff—degrades sharply (FPR 0.595). Training-data recency alone does not rescue parametric verification. The latest-cutoff non-Anthropic model tested (Qwen3-235B: Jun 2025) still ends in the near-ceiling group, so the gap between “seen during training” and “reliably recalled” matters as much as the cutoff. The two later-cutoff Anthropic models (Sonnet 4.6, Opus 4.7) sharpen the point: their inferred cutoffs (Aug 2025, Oct 2025) are not radically later than Qwen3-235B’s, yet their FPR shifts on the supplement are an order of magnitude smaller. Cutoff recency is therefore necessary but insufficient; pipeline-level differences (Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF) for abstention, “I don’t know” calibration) appear to dominate the temporal-robustness story.

Baseline temporal consistency.

For bibtex-updater, detection rates are consistent across temporal segments (±\pm2%); DOI-only improves slightly on newer entries because recent papers more consistently include DOIs.

F.1 Temporal supplement (2024–2025)

The pattern extends past 2024–2025: a 60-entry probe on 2026 arXiv submissions reproduces the FPR multiplier (r=−0.82r{=}-0.82 between baseline aggressiveness and relative post-cutoff degradation).

To validate the 60-entry temporal probe at scale (probe composition in § A.3), we construct a 448-entry temporal supplement: 300 valid entries scraped from DBLP across six ML venues (NeurIPS, ICML, ICLR, AAAI, CVPR, ECCV) for publication years 2024–2025, plus 148 hallucinated entries generated via the standard perturbation pipeline (58/52/38 across Tiers 1/2/3, spanning all 14 types; Tab. 5). This provides 10×10{\times} more valid entries than the probe (300 vs. 30), yielding substantially tighter confidence intervals on FPR estimates. The 448-entry set (300 valid / 148 hallucinated, full coverage) is the canonical temporal supplement reported here; every released prediction file covers the same 448 keys, several of them also carrying rows from the 858-entry superset. A later 858-entry superset of the same 2024–2025 DBLP pool backs the extended reviewer-experiment robustness checks (recall probe, late-cutoff control, GPT-5.1 run-to-run variance) reported separately in the released artifacts (results/reviewer_experiments/FINDINGS.md), and is presented alongside—not in place of—the canonical 448-entry table.

Tab. 28 compares each LLM baseline’s performance on the original benchmark (2021–2023 valid entries) against the temporal supplement (2024–2025 valid entries). The pattern is unambiguous: every model’s FPR increases dramatically on recent papers, while detection rate inflates because models flag nearly everything as hallucinated.

†DeepSeek-R1’s run on this supplement returned 151 of 448 entries as [Error fallback] API failures recorded as UNCERTAIN, and those 151 include all 148 hallucinated entries. Its detection rate, Δ\DeltaDR, F1 and MCC therefore measure the harness rather than the model and we mark them not evaluable (n/e). The FPR of 0.856 is scored over the 297 valid entries the run did answer and is comparable to the other rows.

Endpoint drift between the two collections.

The Sonnet 4.6 and Opus 4.7 rows above are read off the 2026-05-05 collection, while Tab. 1 reports the 2026-09-02 collection. Tab. 29 gives both. The two runs share prompt, split, temperature and seed, so the difference is attributable to the endpoint behind a fixed model name rather than to any change we made. The size of that drift is why the rows above are not mixed: on dev_public the FPR moves +0.034+0.034 (Sonnet) and +0.082+0.082 (Opus) between collections, which is larger than the post-cutoff shift the table is built to measure (−0.007-0.007 and +0.001+0.001). Pairing a September 21–23 figure with a May 24–25 figure would therefore report drift as if it were a temporal effect, and with the signs as they fall here it would read as FPR improving on post-cutoff papers (−0.041-0.041, −0.081-0.081).

The supplement confirms three patterns from the probe, now with substantially greater statistical power, and surfaces a fourth via the later-evaluated models. First, FPR rises sharply on recent papers for most models: GPT-5.1’s FPR climbs from 41.1% to 75.9% (1.8×1.8{\times}); three conservative-baseline models (Gemini Flash ++49.5 pp, Mistral Large ++54.3 pp, Llama 4 Maverick ++61.7 pp) post the largest absolute jumps, while GPT-5.1’s increase is more modest at ++34.8 pp. Second, the detection-rate increases are spurious: the four largest-jump models (Gemini Flash, Mistral Large, Llama 4 Maverick, GPT-5.1) achieve DR ≥0.84{\geq}0.84 on the supplement, but only because they flag nearly everything; F1 falls to ≈0.55{\approx}0.55 (from 0.61–0.77 on dev_public) and MCC to ≈0.25{\approx}0.25, confirming near-random predictions. Third, already-aggressive models stay near-ceiling: DeepSeek-V3.2 (baseline FPR 70.2%) shows only a 5.7 pp increase but ends at 75.9%; Qwen3-VL-235B is the most extreme, climbing 55.1% →\to 88.7%, a new cohort maximum. Fourth, a vendor-/pipeline-correlated subset resists: Claude Sonnet 4.6 (FPR 12.0%) and Opus 4.7 (7.3%) hold; Gemini 2.5 Pro (FPR 25.0%) and a later-cutoff GPT-5.4 (FPR 41.3%) over-flag only moderately: pipeline differences appear to dominate over training recency for the residual gap.

The 60-entry probe, which additionally covered 2026 arXiv submissions, showed the same FPR-multiplier pattern with a strong negative correlation (r=−0.82r=-0.82) between baseline aggressiveness and relative degradation, evidence that the failure mode generalizes beyond 2024–2025 DBLP.

These results establish that LLM citation verification leans heavily on parametric knowledge with a graded temporal boundary near the training cutoff: most models fall into the “flag everything unfamiliar” failure mode for post-cutoff papers. But the partial-to-full resistance from Gemini 2.5 Pro, GPT-5.4, and the two Anthropic models shows this is not a hard structural limit of parametric verification: training-pipeline interventions (post-training calibration, abstention RLHF) can shift the trade-off without retrieval augmentation, even at comparable training cutoffs. We caution against reading the latest-cutoff models’ low post-cutoff FPR as evidence of better calibration: the 2024–2025 supplement is drawn from DBLP proceedings, so for a model whose training data plausibly ingested those same DBLP records, a correct valid verdict is indistinguishable from training-data recall (contamination) rather than principled abstention or verification. We therefore do not attribute their resistance to calibration on this supplement alone: the recall probe and the third-provider control (§ F.4) point toward calibration for Opus 4.7 without excluding recall, and separating the two fully would require post-cutoff valid entries the models provably never saw, which the current supplement cannot guarantee.

F.2 Robustness check: cutoff-aware prompting

S2, Crossref and OpenAlex exhibit weeks-to-months ingestion lag for new arXiv preprints, contributing additively to the post-cutoff FPR rise, while the arXiv API itself covers preprints immediately but not venue-published versions; the empirical confirmation follows.

Mitigation and controls. A cutoff-aware prompting variant (§ F.2) recovers most of GPT-5.1’s post-cutoff FPR (75.9%→0.0%75.9\%{\to}0.0\% on the entries it still commits to) but inflates its abstention uniformly (pre-cutoff uncertain rises to 52.7%52.7\%), whereas on Sonnet 4.6 the same addendum abstains selectively (post-cutoff uncertain 48.9%48.9\% against 8.7%8.7\% pre-cutoff) while halving its committed-entry FPR; the failure is epistemic miscalibration, not structural blindness, and the addendum’s effect is model-dependent. The later-cutoff GPT-5.4 control shows that recency helps but does not cure over-flagging: on these 2024–2025 papers, inside its Aug 2025 window, its FPR is 41.3%41.3\% (§ F.3), well below the earlier-cutoff over-flagging cluster yet far above the latest-cutoff models.

The temporal results above establish H1: LLMs do not know their own cutoff; post-cutoff FPR rises sharply because the model treats unfamiliar papers as suspicious. A separate hypothesis remains untested: H2, that LLMs can route post-cutoff citations to UNCERTAIN if explicitly reminded of the cutoff. H1 and H2 are orthogonal: H1 failing does not imply H2 must fail (the model may have latent metacognitive capacity that the default prompt does not elicit), and H2 failing would upgrade H1 from “epistemic miscalibration” to “structural blindness to temporal uncertainty.”

Prompt addendum.

Each cutoff-aware variant appends the following text to the default verification prompt, verbatim:

⬇
Note: your training data has a knowledge cutoff. If the citation could
post-date your training data, or if you cannot recall the paper with
confidence, respond with UNCERTAIN rather than HALLUCINATED or VALID.
Do not guess.

No other element of the prompt, temperature (T=0T{=}0), seed (42), or token budget (max_completion_tokens=1024, the non-Anthropic value of § B.2.4; Sonnet 4.6 runs through the OpenRouter mirror, which uses the same budget) is changed, so any observed shift in predictions is attributable to the addendum alone.

Subset of models.

We run the cutoff-aware variant on GPT-5.1, Gemini 2.5 Flash, Qwen3-235B, and Claude Sonnet 4.6. DeepSeek-R1 is omitted because its default-prompt run on this supplement failed on 151 of 448 entries (Tab. 28, footnote †\dagger), leaving no usable default-prompt baseline to compare an addendum against; DeepSeek-V3.2 is omitted because it already sits at the aggressive ceiling (FPR 0.759 with DR 0.980), where any measured “improvement” would be dominated by noise. Mistral Large is omitted because its FPR dynamics closely track Qwen3-235B. The Sonnet 4.6 sweep was added later (2026-07-02, through the OpenRouter mirror) with both a cutoff-aware and a same-snapshot default pass on the canonical 448-entry supplement and the 150-entry pre-cutoff sample, so its comparison is fully within-run and unaffected by the endpoint drift of § 5. The four-model subset spans the full conservative–aggressive FPR spectrum observed in Tab. 28: Sonnet 4.6 anchors the calibrated end, Gemini Flash and GPT-5.1 populate the conservative-to-middle range, and Qwen3-235B the aggressive end.

Metrics.

We report FPR and the UNCERTAIN rate (coverage is its complement) per segment, stratified by each model’s training-data cutoff (Tab. 27) into pre-cutoff and post-cutoff entries. The comparison is computed from cached predictions via hallmark.evaluation.temporal.compare_prompt_variants, so the ablation is reproducible from the released prediction dumps without re-running the API calls. The default-prompt FPR baseline here (FPRdef{}_{\text{def}} in Tab. 30) matches the main temporal supplement (Tab. 28) for GPT-5.1, Gemini 2.5 Flash and Qwen3-235B, scored on the same 448 entries; Sonnet 4.6 uses its own 2026-07-02 snapshot (18.6%18.6\% vs. 12.0%12.0\% there), so read its Δ\DeltaFPR within this experiment.

Outcome classification (per model).

The four tested models exhibit qualitatively different outcomes, so a single aggregate classification would obscure the signal.

  • •

    GPT-5.1: FPR drop =75.9=75.9 pp, pre-cutoff UNCERTAIN=52.7=52.7%, post-cutoff UNCERTAIN=94.4=94.4% →\rightarrow mostly blanket abstention: it abstains on 94%94\% of new and 53%53\% of old papers.

  • •

    Gemini 2.5 Flash: FPR drop =12.5=12.5 pp, pre-cutoff UNCERTAIN=0.7=0.7%, post-cutoff UNCERTAIN=19.2=19.2% →\rightarrow strong H1 confirmation.

  • •

    Qwen3-235B: FPR drop =80.9=80.9 pp, pre-cutoff UNCERTAIN=95.3=95.3%, post-cutoff UNCERTAIN=99.8=99.8% →\rightarrow blanket abstention: UNCERTAIN on 9595–100%100\% of entries, old or new, so the FPR drop is not selective.

  • •

    Claude Sonnet 4.6: FPR drop =8.9=8.9 pp (18.6%→9.7%18.6\%\to 9.7\% on committed entries), pre-cutoff UNCERTAIN=8.7=8.7%, post-cutoff UNCERTAIN=48.9=48.9% →\rightarrow selective abstention, the closest to H2 in the cohort.

Sonnet 4.6 comes closest to H2 holds: it is the only model whose abstention inflates selectively—post-cutoff UNCERTAIN rises to 48.9%48.9\% while pre-cutoff abstention stays below 9%9\%—and its committed-entry FPR halves (18.6%→9.7%18.6\%\to 9.7\%). The selectivity still routes roughly half the post-cutoff entries to a human, so abstention remains the mitigation’s price. The other three respond in qualitatively different ways: GPT-5.1 and Qwen3-235B lose discrimination (post-cutoff UNCERTAIN above 94%, with pre-cutoff abstention inflating by 52 pp and 95 pp respectively), while Gemini 2.5 Flash is barely moved by the reminder (FPR drop only 12.5 pp while pre-cutoff UNCERTAIN stays near zero). The practical implication stands: prompt-level temporal-awareness mitigations are not portable across models—the four responses differ qualitatively—and cannot be relied on as a substitute for retrieval-augmented verification.

F.3 Later-cutoff robustness check: GPT-5.4 on the temporal supplement

H1 predicts that the FPR rise on post-cutoff entries is a direct consequence of the training-data cutoff: moving the cutoff forward should shift which entries the model recognizes and, in turn, drop the FPR on entries that cross the new cutoff line. We probe this with a single later-cutoff model: GPT-5.4 (gpt-5.4-2026-03-05), released on 5 March 2026 with an August 31, 2025 training cutoff, roughly 11 months later than GPT-5.1’s September 2024 cutoff. We run it zero-shot on the same 448-entry 2024–2025 temporal supplement used in Tab. 30 and compare entry-by-entry against the existing GPT-5.1 default-prompt predictions. GPT-5.4 is reported here as a single-model temporal-cutoff probe; its zero-shot dev_public performance is also included as a baseline row in Tab. 1. The GPT-5.4 per-entry predictions on all 448 supplement entries are released, so the probe’s aggregate FPR (0.413) and DR (0.899) are reproducible offline without further API calls.

Three features of the result replicate the paper’s temporal narrative across a model generation:

  • •

    FPR drops monotonically with cutoff distance. The 2024-and-earlier stratum shifts from post-cutoff (GPT-5.1) to pre-cutoff (GPT-5.4) and FPR drops by 2828 pp. The 2025 stratum is post-cutoff for both models but is closer to the GPT-5.4 cutoff; FPR drops by 4242 pp, consistent with a graded notion of “unfamiliar” rather than a binary cutoff.

  • •

    GPT-5.4 still over-flags. On pre-cutoff 2024 entries, GPT-5.4’s FPR is 28%28\%, far from zero. Training cutoff alone does not explain the full FPR burden: long-tail recognition, paraphrased titles, and pre-print/published-version mismatches contribute residual false positives even for papers the model’s training data should have covered. This tempers a naïve “just use a newer model” mitigation.

  • •

    UNCERTAIN rate does not rise. Unlike the cutoff-aware prompt ablation (Tab. 30), which inflated abstention without shifting discrimination, moving to a later-cutoff model reduces FPR and drops UNCERTAIN from 2.0%2.0\% to 0.0%0.0\%. The gain comes from familiarity with the newer entries rather than from added caution.

We interpret this as evidence that H1 is a genuine temporal phenomenon rather than an artifact of GPT-5.1 specifically, and that the practical mitigation path is retrieval-augmented verification rather than prompt-engineered abstention, consistent with the agentic-baseline finding in Tab. 1.

F.4 Calibration-vs-memorization controls

Two controls push against, but do not eliminate, the memorization reading (§ F.4). A recall probe finds Opus 4.7 accepts 84%84\% of valid 2024–2025 papers it cannot recall, consistent with calibration rather than memorization; the recall measure is model-derived—we count only papers the model itself reports it cannot recall—so contamination is reduced but not excluded. Sonnet 4.6’s lower FPR is partly recall-driven. A third-provider late-cutoff control (DeepSeek-V4-Pro, complete n=300n{=}300 run at full coverage) holds its post-cutoff FPR at 0.360.36 where GPT-5.1 reaches 0.930.93 on the same entries, consistent with the effect spanning providers without establishing it.44 4 The control supports the cross-provider reading but does not establish it: DeepSeek-V4-Pro matches rather than exceeds the Anthropic cutoffs, it is a single third-party model, and no recall probe was run on it, so contamination is not separable (§ F.4). The resistance points away from pure memorization for Opus 4.7, but with N=2N{=}2 holding models from one provider and a single third-party control, it remains a preliminary signal that stops short of a causal attribution.

Three targeted experiments probe the mechanism behind the temporal-robustness results, using the temporal supplement and a dev_public subsample. Each is reported with its own NN and complements Tab. 28. All three were run on 2026-05-28 through the Hallmark Python API: GPT-5.1 via the native OpenAI endpoint (gpt-5.1), and the Anthropic and DeepSeek models via OpenRouter (anthropic/claude-sonnet-4.6, anthropic/claude-opus-4.7, deepseek/deepseek-v4-pro).

(E1) Recall probe: calibration vs. memorization.

A low post-cutoff FPR on a real paper is ambiguous: the model may be calibrated (declining to flag the unfamiliar) or merely recalling a paper its training data contained. This is the contamination confound noted in § 4.4: the supplement’s valid entries are scraped from DBLP, and a model whose training data ingested those same DBLP records can accept them from memory rather than verification. On 150150 valid 20242024–20252025 papers we run, per model, the standard verifier (FPR) and a recall probe that supplies only the title and year and asks for the author list and venue with no lookup (“recalled” == predicted-author last-name Jaccard ≥0.5\geq 0.5 vs. truth). If a low FPR were memorization-driven, accepted-as-valid verdicts would concentrate on recalled papers.

Opus 4.7 accepts 84%84\% of valid papers it cannot recall, so its low FPR reflects genuine calibration rather than memorization; Sonnet 4.6 accepts 87%87\% of papers it recalls against 50%50\% of those it cannot, but on the latter it abstains on 24%24\% rather than flagging them, so part of the gap is abstention, not memorization; GPT-5.1 recalls none and flags 92%92\%. This partially resolves the contamination confound: it is largely ruled out for Opus 4.7 and only partly for Sonnet 4.6. Caveats: title-given recall is a lower bound on memorization; abstention and “cannot recall” are not perfectly separable; N=150N{=}150, one sample per entry (the GPT-5 endpoint samples stochastically at the requested T=0T{=}0; see E3).

(E2) A third-provider late-cutoff control.

As a check that the FPR resistance is not specific to the Anthropic pipeline, we evaluate DeepSeek-V4-Pro—a third-provider model—on a fixed stratified n=300n{=}300 subsample of the supplement, alongside GPT-5.1 and Sonnet 4.6 re-run on the same entries. This is weaker than the intended control: DeepSeek-V4-Pro matches the Anthropic cutoff rather than exceeding it, and the reading below rests on the cross-model ordering, not its absolute FPR. On the complete run its FPR is 0.360.36 at full coverage (two residual uncertain verdicts; DR 0.870.87), versus 0.930.93 for GPT-5.1 and 0.290.29 for Sonnet 4.6 on the same entries, and its year breakdown (0.290.29 on 2024 entries, 0.450.45 on 2025) shows the same graded recency pattern as the cohort. The absolute levels here sit above Tab. 28 (e.g. Sonnet 0.29 vs. 0.120) because this control ran on a later endpoint snapshot and an n=300n{=}300 subsample; we read the within-run cross-model ordering, not the level (§ 5). A non-Anthropic model thus also resists the post-cutoff FPR rise, consistent with the effect tracking training recency across providers. Caveats: a single third-party control; provider-reported cutoff; contamination is not separable for this model (no recall probe run on it).

(E3) Run-to-run variance at the GPT-5 endpoint.

We send gpt-5.1 temperature=0.0, but the GPT-5 endpoint samples stochastically regardless of the requested value, so each baseline run is one stochastic draw. Three independent GPT-5.1 runs on a fixed n=150n{=}150 dev_public subsample give F1 =0.815±0.002=0.815\pm 0.002, FPR =0.528±0.009=0.528\pm 0.009, DR =0.965±0.000=0.965\pm 0.000 (mean ±\pm sample std; 1/1501/150 label flips). The F1 run-to-run std (0.0020.002) is far below the Sonnet 4.6−-GPT-5.1 F1 gap (0.1270.127, ≈60×{\approx}60\times), so single-run rankings are stable to sampling noise. Caveat: N=3N{=}3 runs; n=150n{=}150 subsample.

F.5 Thinking-budget regime boundary

Motivation.

The main-table baselines all share a fixed max_completion_tokens budget (1024 tokens on the OpenAI/OpenRouter endpoints, including the chain-of-thought DeepSeek-R1 baseline; 256 on the Anthropic native endpoint; see § B.2.4). At this budget, the structured JSON-output contract holds across the entire cohort. Three families of post-snapshot thinking-tier models break this contract—Gemini 3.1 Pro/Flash-Lite, DeepSeek-V4, and Qwen3.5—emitting chain-of-thought scratchpad before the verdict and exhausting the budget mid-reasoning. During the codebase additions for the Q2 2026 frontier cohort we observed concrete failure modes that motivated their exclusion from the main table:

  • •

    google/gemini-3.1-pro-preview: unbounded thinking tokens overrun the 1024-token max_completion_tokens budget, causing JSON parse failures across nearly all entries; google/gemini-2.5-pro (which also thinks by default, but mostly completes within the 1024-token budget) is the closest reliable substitute and is included in the main table.

  • •

    google/gemini-3.1-flash-lite-preview: supports the full thinking range (minimal→\tohigh); same unbounded-thinking risk as gemini-3.1-pro-preview.

  • •

    qwen/qwen3.5-397b-a17b: ∼40%{\sim}40\% empty responses (thinking mode consumed the budget before the JSON object closed).

  • •

    qwen/qwen3.5-122b-a10b: parses successfully but emits 500+ reasoning tokens per reply, inflating cost ∼5×{\sim}5\times versus the matched non-thinking baseline.

  • •

    deepseek/deepseek-v4-pro and deepseek-v4-flash: thinking models with reasoning_effort levels high/xhigh supported; same budget-exhaustion risk as the V3-R1 chain-of-thought baseline at 1024 tokens.

Smoke-test design.

To quantify the regime boundary rather than assert it, we run a stratified n=100n{=}100 subsample of dev_public (proportional across the 11 main hallucination types, ≥5\geq 5 entries per type, fixed seed) on three post-snapshot models under two budget regimes:

Reported metrics.

Per (model, regime) cell we report DR, FPR, F1, MCC, parse-failure rate (PF) (fraction of entries whose response is missing or non-JSON), mean and p95 output tokens, and $/entry. Cost is computed at the OpenRouter listed rate as of 2026-05-04.

Results.

Tab. 34 reports parse-failure rate, saturation ratio p95/capp_{95}/\text{cap}, and full classification metrics for all nine (model, regime) cells; Tab. 35 gives the per-type detection-rate breakdown.

Three archetypes of regime-boundary behavior.

The smoke test reveals three qualitatively distinct responses to budget headroom:

  • •

    Clean ceiling (GPT-5.5). Saturation 1.00 →\to 1.00 →\to 0.34 across the three regimes; parse-failure rate falls 66% →\to 12% →\to 1%; F1 climbs 0.18 →\to 0.72 →\to 0.78. The model has an implicit reasoning trace that consumes the entire max_completion_tokens budget at 256, and its capability is fully recovered at 4k. This is the textbook regime-boundary behavior.

  • •

    Budget-filling (Gemini 3.1 Pro). Saturation 0.998 →\to 0.969 →\to 0.964 from 2k to 16k; mean output grows monotonically (834 →\to 1183 →\to 1688) and the worst-case reasoning trace tracks the cap rather than converging to a fixed length. F1 is essentially flat (0.79 // 0.77 // 0.78) and parse failure stays at ≤1%\leq 1\%, so the cap is not biting in absolute terms. Because its thinking budget was set to half the cap in every cell, output length grows with the cap by design; whether the model limits itself would need a test that raises the cap while keeping the thinking budget fixed. The extra thinking does not help either: F1 stays flat and parse failures stay at or below 1%1\%.

  • •

    Clean recovery (DeepSeek-V4-Pro). Saturation 1.00 →\to 0.37 →\to 0.21; F1 0.75 →\to 0.82 →\to 0.78. Recovers cleanly at 8k under reasoning_effort=high, and 16k adds nothing. Best-cell F1 (0.82) is competitive with the main-table cohort.

Reading the table.

None of the three models would have replaced a main-table baseline in expectation: their best-cell F1 (GPT-5.5: 0.78; Gemini 3.1 Pro: 0.79; DeepSeek-V4-Pro: 0.82) sits in the existing cohort’s mid-range, comfortably under the cohort-leading independent F1 (Sonnet 4.6’s 0.8930.893). The protocol-budget concern is empirically resolved for two of three: GPT-5.5 and DeepSeek-V4-Pro reach a clean budget ceiling and fit the fixed-budget protocol once we know what budget to allocate. The third (Gemini 3.1 Pro) fills whatever thinking budget it is given: its cost grows with the budget ($1.34 →\to $2.62 per 100 entries) while F1 stays flat. More generally, a fair fixed-budget benchmark must either (i) allocate the highest budget needed by any one model (inflating cost ∼10×{\sim}10\times across the cohort), or (ii) use a budget at which the JSON contract holds for all listed models and exclude models that cannot answer within it. We choose (ii) and report the boundary explicitly.

Cost and wall-clock.

The full nine-cell smoke test cost $10.77 at OpenRouter list prices (May 2026) and consumed ∼\sim303 wall-clock minutes (most of which was DeepSeek-V4-Pro’s chain-of-thought latency). Scaling to full dev_public (n=1,119n{=}1{,}119) at the same price ratios costs ∼$120{\sim}\$120, well within a typical per-paper evaluation budget. Wall-clock per cell is ∼\sim10–65 s/entry depending on tier and budget; cells parallelize across providers without contention.

Appendix G bibtex-updater: the co-designed reference tool

This section collects everything on bibtex-updater, the co-designed reference tool: its implementation (§ G.1), its benchmark evaluation and the co-design-bias controls (§ G.2), and a tool-augmented LLM baseline (§ G.2).

G.1 Implementation

We additionally describe bibtex-updater, a co-developed open-source citation verification tool designed for deployment by venues, reviewers, and authors: not to optimize benchmark scores, but to provide reliable, automated checking that integrates into existing publication workflows.

G.1.1 Design goals

Three practical requirements drive the design:

  1. 1.

    Zero human effort. Verification must be fully automated: no manual review, no prompt engineering, no LLM inference costs. This rules out approaches requiring human-in-the-loop validation or expensive API calls to language models.

  2. 2.

    Workflow integration. The tool must integrate into existing pipelines: CI/CD (GitHub Actions), pre-commit hooks, Overleaf builds, and one-off command-line checks. A tool that requires a separate platform or manual invocation will not be adopted.

  3. 3.

    Graceful degradation. When APIs are unavailable or rate-limited, the tool should return partial results rather than fail silently. Venues processing hundreds of submissions cannot tolerate flaky infrastructure.

G.1.2 Verification pipeline

bibtex-updater implements a multi-stage pipeline that processes each BibTeX entry through increasingly expensive checks:

Pre-API validation (zero cost).

Before any network calls, the tool checks for syntactic red flags: DOIs that fail to resolve (HEAD request to doi.org, counting only doi.org’s own rejection as non-resolution—a publisher-side block or bot-mitigation status reached after a successful redirect is not evidence the DOI is absent, and a versioned arXiv DOI is normalized to its unversioned form first), future publication years, implausible dates (<1800<1800), and malformed fields. These cheap checks catch Tier 1 hallucinations without API overhead.

Multi-source lookup.

The tool queries Crossref, DBLP, and Semantic Scholar using title and first-author search, and resolves arXiv IDs against the arXiv Atom API for preprint-specific consistency checks. Each source returns candidate records that are scored using a weighted combination of fuzzy title matching (70%, token-sort ratio) and author Jaccard similarity (30%). The best-scoring candidate across all sources is selected for field-by-field comparison.

Post-match analysis.

Once a candidate is identified, the tool compares DOI, title, authors, year, and venue against the input entry. Venue comparison uses alias-aware matching for 17 major ML/AI venues (e.g., NeurIPS/NIPS, ICML, ICLR, CVPR), so that name variations within that set do not trigger false positives; ISO-4 journal abbreviations outside it (ACM Trans. Graph., Proc. Natl. Acad. Sci. U.S.A.) fall below the match threshold and were a substantial false-positive source in the version evaluated here. A dedicated preprint detection stage queries Semantic Scholar to identify entries that claim venue publication when only an arXiv preprint exists.

Status assignment.

Each entry receives one status code. Thirteen occur on dev_public: verified (442), unconfirmed (147), swapped_authors (146), partial_match (85), venue_mismatch (66), not_found (52), doi_not_found (46), doi_mismatch (36), future_date (30), arxiv_id_mismatch (18), year_mismatch (17), title_mismatch (14) and given_name_substitution (13). The 147 unconfirmed verdicts are where most of the tool’s abstention sits. The HALLMARK wrapper maps these to binary labels and confidence scores for benchmark evaluation.

G.1.3 Deployment modes

The tool supports three deployment scenarios: CI/CD integration (--strict flag exits with nonzero code on detection, gating submission workflows), pre-commit hooks (validates .bib files on every commit), and batch processing (concurrent workers with rate limiting for venue-scale use). For venue-scale deployment, we recommend a two-stage workflow: run bibtex-updater to flag suspicious citations, then manual review of high-confidence flags (confidence ≥0.7\geq 0.7); at a 2%2\% base rate expect roughly one true hallucination per four flags, and read that as the optimistic end—at 1%1\% it is one per seven and at 0.5%0.5\% one per thirteen, and the prevalence we measured on real submissions was indistinguishable from zero (§§ E.1 and 5). At NeurIPS scale (approximately 10,000 submissions, approximately 50 references each) that is half a million references. At the throughput we measure with keys, credentials and a 20-per-minute pace (2.42.4 s per entry) eight workers need roughly 4242 hours; at the wrapper’s older rate limit (5.75.7 s per entry) roughly 9999. The tool requires no GPU or LLM API keys and is MIT-licensed; code is publicly available at https://github.com/rpatrik96/hallmark.

G.2 Evaluation and co-design bias

bibtex-updater (Reizinger, 2025) is a multi-database cross-referencing tool co-developed alongside this benchmark. Its results appear in Tab. 1 under the “Co-designed (reference upper bound)” section, separated from independent tools by a rule. We include it in the main table to give a complete picture of the recall–precision spectrum: bibtex-updater anchors the precision end by flagging conservatively (DR 0.820, FPR 0.051), not by topping detection rate, and it abstains on the ∼12{\sim}12–14%14\% of entries it cannot verify against a backing record (coverage 0.860.86 dev / 0.880.88 test), an abstention that recovers recall; the low FPR comes from conservative matching, not from abstaining. The explicit upper-bound label and this appendix keep the comparison transparent. The co-design relationship means the benchmark taxonomy and sub-test structure were informed by the tool’s detection capabilities, creating a potential circularity that could inflate its apparent performance; readers should treat its numbers as an informative upper bound, not a fair head-to-head comparison with independent tools.

Per-type breakdown for bibtex-updater.

Tab. 37 shows per-type detection rates for bibtex-updater. It detects perfectly (a per-type detection rate of 1.000; parenthesized values throughout this passage) on fabricated_doi, placeholder_authors, future_date, chimeric_title, hybrid_fabrication, plausible_fabrication, and merged_citation, and stays strong on swapped_authors (0.985) and near_miss_title (0.885). The weakest types are precisely those where the tool abstains rather than guesses—partial_author_list (0.219), nonexistent_venue (0.436), preprint_as_pub. (0.677), wrong_venue (0.447), and arxiv_version_mismatch (0.612)—where a could-not-verify verdict is scored as VALID in this forced-binary detection rate (the abstention behavior of § E.2). These cells are scored from the tool’s per-entry verdicts on the released labels, the same verdicts behind the aggregate in Tab. 36.

Readers should interpret bibtex-updater’s results with caution: (1) its multi-database verification strategy was developed concurrently with the benchmark design; (2) the sub-test structure mirrors the tool’s internal verification pipeline; (3) the pre-screening layer was designed to complement its known blind spots. We encourage independent tool developers to submit evaluations via Hallmark’s contribution framework to establish unbiased baselines.

One observation bounds the circularity concern from the other side. The ground-truth audit recovered 52 real papers (27 dev_public, 25 test_public) that earlier labeling had wrongly marked HALLUCINATED. On 40 of those 52—19 of 27 on dev_public and 21 of 25 on test_public—bibtex-updater’s database cross-check returned VALID, diverging from the then-current (buggy) labels rather than tracking them; it agreed with the buggy label on the remaining 12. A tool whose apparent accuracy were merely an artifact of co-design would mirror the benchmark’s labels, including their errors, so a majority divergence is evidence that its detections rest on external database evidence rather than on the label distribution. It is evidence and not proof: 12 entries went the other way. The tool abstains on entries it cannot back with a record, reporting dev_public DR 0.820 / FPR 0.051 / F1 0.880 (Tab. 36), and the relabel removed an artifact that had flattered the more aggressive LLM verifiers more than the rule-based tool (§ 4.3).

Cross-domain probe.

The released test_crossdomain split (500 entries: 200 valid / 300 hallucinated; composition in § A.3) evaluates bibtex-updater v1.2.0 outside the ML-venue regime the main splits sample. Detection transfers: DR reaches 0.890, against 0.820 on dev_public. The released split reports FPR 0.375 (Tab. 38), but two confounds inflate that number. First, the split’s valid biomedical entries are all dated 2026, post-cutoff for every LLM (the recency confound we take up below); bibtex-updater queries live databases and carries no cutoff, so this does not affect its own verdicts. Second, and specific to the rule-based tool, our biomedical scrape carried metadata noise—Vancouver-style author initials, epub-versus-print year ambiguity, preprint venue strings—that its exact-match verification reads as contradictions and flags, manufacturing false positives that reflect the citation record rather than the tool’s judgment. A recency-matched, canonically-resolved rebuild removes both: 152 valid biomedical entries from 2021–2023, each field replaced by the CrossRef record its DOI resolves to (canonical author, year, venue), plus the same three hallucination tiers. On that clean split bibtex-updater’s headline FPR is 0.112, about twice its in-domain 0.051, though it commits to only 29% of the valid biomedical entries, abstaining on the other 71% (against 14% in-domain). The canonical metadata converts the released split’s mis-flags into honest abstentions: out of domain the tool abstains rather than over-flags, because its ML-tuned assumptions (full author names, one canonical year, exact venue strings) cannot confirm biomedical records against its backing databases. The cost of leaving the regime is coverage, not precision (Tab. 38).

Recovering coverage with a Stage-2 diagnoser.

bibtex-updater’s out-of-domain abstention is a coverage gap that a second stage can fill. We run the paper’s two-stage cascade on the matched split: Stage 1 bibtex-updater decides the 263 entries it can confirm or refute and defers the 189 it cannot to Stage 2, an agentic Sonnet 4.6 diagnoser (up to five tool calls per entry).55 5 Stage 1 is served from the persisted standalone verdicts; re-running bibtex-check live hangs on arXiv DOI HEAD checks against the fabricated future-dated DOIs, so the live cascade is impractical here. Stage 2 is a dated OpenRouter snapshot (§ B.2.4). Stage 2 recovers the coverage: the cascade commits on all 152 valid biomedical entries (valid-entry coverage 0.29→1.000.29\to 1.00) at FPR 0.189 and DR 0.975 (F1 0.941; the aggressive stance is nearly identical at FPR 0.211, since Stage 2 leaves almost nothing uncertain). Closing the coverage gap costs little precision—headline FPR 0.112 with bibtex-updater abstaining, 0.189 with the cascade committing on everything—and stays well below the recall-aggressive models’ over-flagging (Qwen3-235B 0.974): out of domain, the abstention is recoverable.

The LLM cohort: domain versus recency.

The zero-shot LLM verifiers of Tab. 1 were unevaluated cross-domain; we run eleven of them on both the released 2026 biomedical entries and the recency-matched rebuild, which turns the released split’s confound into a clean 2×22\times 2 over domain and recency (Tab. 39).66 6 DeepSeek-R1 is excluded: 432 of its 500 cross-domain predictions are [Error fallback] API failures (86%86\%), so no metric on that split measures the model. The released split’s high biomedical FPR is a post-cutoff artifact: 89% of the biomedical false positives there give the future date as the reason (“2026 is in the future,” “beyond my training cutoff”), and on the recency-matched entries—same domain, pre-cutoff—that share falls to 2%, with the remaining false positives turning into genuine recall failures (an unresolvable DOI, an unfamiliar venue). The residual pure-domain effect (matched FPR minus dev_public FPR, recency held fixed) is model-dependent: negative or small for the calibrated verifiers (GPT-5.1 −0.31-0.31, GPT-5.4 −0.12-0.12, Sonnet 4.6 −0.03-0.03, Opus 4.7 +0.05+0.05, Gemini 2.5 Pro −0.03-0.03, Llama 4 Maverick −0.09-0.09), and large only for a recall-aggressive model (Qwen3-235B +0.44+0.44), which flags legitimate bioRxiv preprints cited in article form as fabrications. Biomedical citations are not inherently harder to verify: the cross-domain FPR rise was recency, and what domain adds is small except where a model already over-flags in its own regime.

Provider content filtering on biomedical citations.

Both Anthropic models we query through OpenRouter (Claude Opus 4.7 and Sonnet 4.6) return an empty, content-filtered response (finish_reason: content_filter) on the same 5 of 152 valid biomedical entries (3.3%) in the recency-matched split: all virology and immunology papers on SARS-CoV-2 inhibitor resistance, ACE2 receptor-binding and antibody-escape mutations, and HIV envelope neutralization, i.e. dual-use–adjacent titles the provider filter blocks. The refusal is deterministic: it reproduces at completion budgets from 512 to 4096 tokens, so it is not output truncation, and a trivial control prompt to the same endpoint returns normally, so it is not an outage or a credit fault. These entries fall to the verifier’s error path and score as UNCERTAIN, i.e. committed-VALID under our convention, so they do not inflate false-positive rates. They do depress detection: the same error path catches 10 hallucinated entries for Opus and 9 for Sonnet, which then score as missed detections, so the cost is one of availability for the FPR column and of accuracy for the DR column. The released prediction dumps record every one of these records as [Error fallback] Parse error: None, indistinguishable there from a generic API failure; the content_filter finish reason was observed at run time and is not recoverable from the release. The filter never fires on the ML-venue core, so the failure mode is invisible in-domain and surfaces only out of domain: a deployment consideration specific to safety-filtered providers, orthogonal to the verdict-quality question the rest of this section studies.

Tool-augmented LLM baseline.

To test whether combining LLM reasoning with API-backed verification is greater than the sum of its parts, we augment GPT-5.1 with bibtex-updater’s structured output. For each entry, we first run bibtex-check to obtain the verification status, mismatched fields, confidence score, and APIs consulted, then inject this evidence into an augmented prompt that instructs the model to use the tool findings as evidence while applying its own judgment. Tab. 40 compares the augmented model against its components.

The augmented model improves over standalone GPT-5.1 on every headline metric: detection rate rises slightly (84.3% vs. 83.7%) while FPR drops sharply (0.144 vs. 0.411) and ECE improves to 0.078, the best calibration of any baseline. However, it still falls short of bibtex-updater’s standalone FPR (0.144 vs. 0.051).

Tab. 41 reveals why. On the two types where bibtex-updater excels and GPT-5.1 struggles—swapped_authors and near_miss_title—the augmented model tracks the LLM rather than the tool: swapped_authors reaches 47.8% against bibtex-updater’s 98.5% (standalone GPT-5.1: 44.8%), and near_miss_title falls from the LLM’s own 57.7% to 50.0% against the tool’s 88.5%. The LLM overrides tool-detected metadata mismatches, treating them as potential API artifacts rather than genuine hallucination signals. The one type where evidence injection buys anything is chimeric_title, which rises to 97.9% from standalone GPT-5.1’s 89.4%: the tool evidence helps the LLM confirm an existing suspicion rather than revise a judgment. On three types—fabricated_doi, near_miss_title and plausible_fabrication—the augmented model lands below both of its components at once.

These results demonstrate that naïve evidence injection—presenting tool output as LLM context—is insufficient to realize the complementarity between parametric and retrieval-based verification. The LLM treats tool evidence as advisory rather than authoritative, defaulting to its own judgment when conflicts arise. More structured integration strategies—such as forcing acceptance of tool-detected field mismatches, weighted ensembling, or agentic tool-use where the LLM iteratively queries APIs—may better combine the complementary strengths.

Appendix H Robustness ablations

We report four ablations that probe whether the precision-ceiling finding is an artifact of a single design choice—a prompt, a threshold, an input field, or a single annotator—alongside the selective-prediction analysis of § E.2. We read all four as robustness evidence for the ranking, not as tuning for best numbers: the tool ranking is what transfers across the regimes these ablations vary (§ 4.3)—it does not survive a change in what counts as a hallucination, which § H.1 measures separately—so we test its invariance to phrasing (§ H.2), operating point (§ H.4), input format (§ H.5), and rater (§ H.6).

H.1 What counts as a hallucination changes the ranking

Four of the fourteen types label entries whose cited work exists. wrong_venue assigns a real paper to the wrong conference, preprint_as_published cites a real preprint as though it appeared at a venue, partial_author_list truncates a real author list without marking it, and arxiv_version_mismatch cites a real preprint with the wrong venue and a shifted year. In each case the reference points at a work a reader can find; what is wrong is the description. The other ten types cover works that do not exist. A verifier that flags all fourteen is doing two jobs, and the benchmark scores them as one.

The distinction is not marginal. On test_public the four modes are 139 of 519 hallucinated entries (26.8%26.8\%), and on dev_public 158 of 606 (26.1%26.1\%). They are not confined to stress_test, and the stress split is 61.5%61.5\% real-paper modes in its own right.

We re-score all 20 tool configurations three ways (Tab. 42): as shipped; with the four modes folded out of the evaluation set entirely; and with them scored as false accusations, so a flag on one counts against the tool. The ranking is stable to neither. Folding them out moves 12 of 20 configurations in rank; scoring them as false accusations moves 16 of 20 and changes the leader. The cascade of Tab. 1 leads as shipped at MCC 0.9410.941 (0.9380.938 conservative) and falls to 0.6680.668 (0.6650.665) as false accusations; bibtex-updater falls less, from 0.7380.738 to 0.6880.688, and takes first place under that reading. Folded out, the cascade keeps its lead (0.9360.936 against 0.8450.845). The reversal has a plain cause, visible in the tools’ detection rates on the four modes alone: the cascade catches nearly all of them (0.9930.993) while bibtex-updater catches 0.5970.597 and DOI-only 0.0650.065. More of the cascade’s headline credit comes from flagging papers that exist.

A second control bounds how much verification those detections require. A classifier with access only to surface features—which fields are present, how long the strings are, how many authors there are, whether the venue string says arXiv, the entry type, the year—and no network access and no semantics reaches DR 0.4680.468 at FPR 0.0450.045 on dev_public and DR 0.3880.388 at FPR 0.0960.096 on test_public, against a majority-class baseline of 0.0000.000. Of the four modes’ positives 80%80\% are perturbations of real entries, while 95%95\% of the valid entries they are scored against were scraped from real bibliographies, so roughly 40%40\% of the separation is a property of how the entries were made rather than of what they claim.

We report this rather than relabel. Which of the four modes a deployed verifier should flag depends on what the verifier is for: a venue chair screening for fabricated citations wants the ten fabrication modes, while a copy-editing pass wants all fourteen. The benchmark as released serves the second reading, and Tab. 1 should be read as a ranking under it. Readers with the first use in mind should take the folded-out column, where the cascade still leads bibtex-updater (0.9360.936 against 0.8450.845). Public venue guidance does not agree on this line. ICML 2026’s area-chair instructions count a reference as hallucinated only when no document with a title anywhere near it can be found, and exclude a real venue that is incorrect for the reference, a swapped author list, and a few missing authors (ICML, 2026): wrong_venue, preprint_as_published and arxiv_version_mismatch fall on the excluded side, and partial_author_list does when the truncation is small. ICLR 2026’s review retrospective instead describes flagged references as ones that “referred to documents that didn’t exist and/or contained egregiously incorrect bibliographic information” (ICLR, 2026), merging the two classes, and ACL 2026 lists hallucinated references as grounds for desk rejection without defining them (ACL, 2026). We therefore report both readings rather than choosing one.

The temporal-mechanism probes (the recall and late-cutoff controls, cutoff-aware prompting, and the thinking-budget boundary) live with failure mode (iii) in Appx. F; the bootstrap CIs are in § B.1. The prompt-variant, field-leave-one-out (LOO), and rater runs use a fresh dated OpenRouter snapshot (2026-05-31) that does not reproduce the main-run absolute aggregates; we therefore read each as a within-run difference, robust to endpoint drift (§ 5).

H.2 Prompt-sensitivity sweep

We sweep four prompt variants—default (the paper’s prompt), notaxo (taxonomy removed), uncertain (abstention explicitly encouraged), and terse (compressed instructions)—over four models on a stratified n=150n{=}150 dev_public sample (81 hallucinated / 69 valid), at temperature 0 and seed 42 (Tab. 43); GPT-5.1 runs through its OpenAI-direct endpoint, the other three through OpenRouter.

The finding is two-part. First, the model ranking is prompt-invariant: mean pairwise Spearman ρ=0.90\rho=0.90 for F1, DR, and FPR across the four variants (Sonnet 4.6 >> GPT-5.1 >> DeepSeek-V3.2 >> Gemini 2.5 Flash on F1 at default), and the sole departure from ρ=1.0\rho=1.0 is a 0.0010.001 F1 near-tie between GPT-5.1 (0.7940.794) and Sonnet 4.6 (0.7930.793) under the uncertain variant: a tie, not a reordering. This is the result that defends the single-prompt design of § 4.2. Second, the absolute FPR is wording-sensitive: GPT-5.1 shows the largest swing: FPR 0.5800.580 at default down to 0.2120.212 under terse (−36.8-36.8 pp), with its UNCERTAIN rate reaching 19.3%19.3\% under uncertain (from 0%0\%). The abstention-encouraging uncertain variant drops Sonnet 4.6’s FPR from 0.1210.121 to 0.0150.015 (−10.6-10.6 pp) and DeepSeek-V3.2’s from 0.8990.899 to 0.6000.600 (−29.9-29.9 pp), while Gemini 2.5 Flash moves only −4.3-4.3 pp. Sonnet’s UNCERTAIN rate rises from 2.0%2.0\% (notaxo/terse) to 8.7%8.7\% (uncertain), a ∼7{\sim}7 pp coverage swing from wording alone. Pooled over all models and non-default variants, the verdict-flip rate against the default is 17.4%17.4\% (all entries) and 13.6%13.6\% when UNCERTAIN-involving flips are excluded, with GPT-5.1 the most prompt-sensitive model (25.8%25.8\% mean flip).

The practical consequence is a scope bound on the post-cutoff FPR magnitude: because a single wording change can move FPR by 1010–3737 pp, we treat the absolute post-cutoff false-alarm rate (§ 4.4) as prompt-conditional and rest the temporal claim on the cross-regime ranking, which this sweep shows is prompt-invariant.

H.3 GEPA prompt optimization

The robustness check above bounds how far wording moves the metrics; it does not say how far a deliberate search through wording can move them. That question is sharpened by failure mode (iii): the cutoff experiments show post-cutoff over-flagging (§ 4.4), the cutoff-aware check shows part of it answers to instructions (§ F.2), and the sweep prices wording high enough to cover the FPR gap between a small model and the frontier (§ H.2). If a prompt is worth that much, the precision gap we report might be a prompting effect rather than a capability difference. We test that directly, and the answer is no.

We optimize the paper’s verification prompt with Genetic-Pareto (GEPA), a reflective evolutionary search that mutates a prompt from natural-language feedback on its own failures (Agrawal et al., 2026). The seed is the paper’s default prompt (§ B.2.3) and the model is Claude Haiku 4.5. The objective is balanced binary accuracy on a 200200-entry dev_public validation set and under-flagging is penalized as hard as over-flagging; uncertain scores 00. Optimization touched dev_public only; every number below is test_public, which the optimizer never saw.

Optimization works, but does not close the gap. Claude Opus 4.7 on the untuned default prompt catches far more hallucinations than the optimized small model at a similar false-positive rate (DR 0.9000.900 vs. 0.7460.746, FPR 0.2050.205 vs. 0.2240.224) on the same split (Tab. 9). Prompt optimization does not move a small model to the frontier’s operating point. We state the claim no more broadly than that: only Haiku was optimized, and it is compared against frontier models running the shared default prompt, so this is an optimized-vs-default comparison.

A note on protocol, since prompt optimizers leak by default. The reflection step sees per-entry feedback on failures, which is an easy channel for the optimizer to write dataset specifics into the prompt. We therefore constrain reflection to describe failure patterns in general terms and forbid it from copying author names, titles, citation keys, or split statistics. The optimized prompt is released as results/gepa_haiku/guarded/best_prompt.txt.

H.4 Threshold and aggregation ablation

We re-score the stored per-entry confidences on dev_public (no API calls) to test two operating-point choices: the decision threshold and the field-aggregation rule (Tab. 45).

Threshold.

Confidences are effectively quantized, so threshold tuning buys almost nothing: the gap between the default 0.50.5 threshold and the best-F1 threshold is below 0.350.35 pp for seven of eight tools ( GPT-5.4 0.340.34 pp, Opus 4.7 0.200.20 pp, Sonnet 4.6 0.090.09 pp, the rest ≤0.07{\leq}0.07 pp). The lone exception is Gemini 2.5 Flash (8.228.22 pp), and it buys F1 only by trading FPR up to 0.3430.343. AUROC orders the verifiers as expected (Sonnet 0.9270.927, Opus 0.9030.903, GPT-5.4 0.8340.834, then the recall-aggressive open-weight models 0.610.61–0.740.74). For the seven quantized-confidence tools the fixed-0.50.5 operating point of Tab. 1 is therefore near-optimal—best-F1 is chosen in-sample on dev_public, so this lower-bounds the true headroom—while Gemini 2.5 Flash is the exception noted above. The ranking is threshold-robust regardless, in contrast to peer benchmarks that hard-code an unjustified match threshold.

Aggregation.

The benchmark’s detector flags an entry when any one of the cross-database sub-tests fails (the “any-miss” rule—the benchmark’s internal detector, distinct from the agentic harness’s any-no-match rule in Appx. D). Sweeping stricter quorums trades DR for FPR monotonically: on the structured sub-tests, any-miss gives DR 0.9500.950 / FPR 0.0000.000, while requiring two, three, or all four misses reduces DR to 0.2690.269, 0.0480.048, 0.0020.002; on the field-level resolver the same sweep drops DR from 0.7590.759 (any-miss) to 0.1280.128 (unanimous). A noisy-voter ensemble makes the same point with real verifiers: treating the twelve zero-shot LLMs with stored per-entry predictions (Tab. 11) as twelve independent voters, flagging whenever any single voter flags reproduces the any-no-match profile (DR 0.9950.995 / FPR 0.8810.881), simple majority (≥7/12\geq 7/12) gives DR 0.7790.779 / FPR 0.1910.191 / F1 0.8030.803, and supermajority and unanimity buy lower FPR at steep DR cost. The benchmark deploys the any-miss rule (F1 0.9750.975); requiring cross-database agreement instead nudges F1 to 0.9850.985 at a small false-positive cost (FPR 0.000→0.0350.000\to 0.035), so any-miss sits within 11 pp of the family’s F1 maximum while holding FPR at zero.

H.5 Input-format and field leave-one-out

We test whether detection rests on a surface format tell or on field content by varying the input representation (full BibTeX vs. structured fields) and dropping one field at a time (title / authors / venue / year / DOI), on the same n=150n{=}150 stratified sample with two models (Tab. 46). This is the dynamic counterpart to the static format-tell audit (§ C.5.4).

Two results. Title carries most of the signal. For Gemini 2.5 Flash, dropping the title raises FPR by +35.5+35.5 pp over the structured baseline (0.145→0.5000.145\to 0.500) and dropping authors by +18.8+18.8 pp, while venue, year, and DOI move FPR little; DeepSeek-V3.2—already near-saturated at FPR 0.810.81 structured—shows the same direction at smaller magnitude (+12.9+12.9 pp for title). Format matters less than content: switching between full BibTeX and structured fields shifts DR/FPR by at most 7.47.4/14.514.5 pp. Detection therefore leans on title and author semantics rather than a surface artifact, reinforcing the construct-validity argument that the result is not driven by a single co-designed field or by formatting (§§ G.2 and C.5.4).

H.6 Multi-rater reliability proxy

This is an automated multi-rater reliability proxy, not human inter-annotator agreement. Three independent LLM raters (Sonnet 4.6, DeepSeek-V3.2, Gemini 2.5 Pro) label 132 blinded entries—80 real-world-incident hallucinations and the 52 relabel-recovered real papers—and we report their agreement (UNCERTAIN mapped to HALLUCINATED, binary; Tab. 47). It does not substitute for human Inter-Annotator Agreement (IAA), which remains future work (§ 5); it serves to test whether independent raters reproduce the relabel.

Overall agreement is only fair: Fleiss’ κ=0.24\kappa=0.24 (Fleiss, 1971) on the “fair” band of the Landis–Koch scale (Landis & Koch, 1977), with pairwise Cohen’s κ\kappa ranging from 0.450.45 (Sonnet–DeepSeek, moderate) down to 0.030.03 (DeepSeek–Gemini Pro, slight). Against the corrected ground-truth labels—the database-backed labels after the relabel audit (§ A.3)—DeepSeek-V3.2 agrees best (κ=0.716\kappa=0.716, accuracy 0.8710.871) and Gemini 2.5 Pro worst (κ=0.026\kappa=0.026); the majority vote reaches accuracy 0.7200.720 (κ=0.340\kappa=0.340).

The diagnostic split is the point. Majority-vote accuracy is 0.9750.975 on the 80 real-world hallucinations but only 0.3270.327 on the 52 relabel-recovered real papers: the LLM raters confidently agree on genuine fabrications yet systematically over-flag the recovered real papers, the same over-flagging failure mode Hallmark is built to measure. Independent raters would have repeated the original labeling error, which both corroborates that the relabel audit corrected a real bias and motivates the precision-via-abstention contribution (§ E.2).

Appendix I Extended limitations

The seven paragraphs below are the full-length limitations discussion that § 5 ranks and compresses.

Dataset scale and coverage.

The benchmark is small relative to the full diversity of citation hallucinations. At 2,526 entries, most types on dev_public and test_public clear ≥30\geq 30 instances—enough for meaningful per-type comparison—but a few fall below it, and test_hidden does not reach the floor at all (§ B.1). Prevalence differs across splits (54.2–62.5%), so we emphasize the prevalence-independent metrics (DR, FPR). We cover English-language BibTeX from five ML venues (2021–2023); the taxonomy and sub-tests are designed to be domain-agnostic but validated mainly in that regime. A 500-entry cross-domain split (PubMed/bioRxiv plus non-ML CS venues), together with a recency-matched, canonically-resolved rebuild, separates domain from post-cutoff recency out of regime (§ G.2). The separation reframes the result: the released split’s apparent cross-domain FPR rise is mostly a recency artifact—the LLMs flag 2026 dates as impossible—and once entries are pre-cutoff the residual domain effect is negative or small for the calibrated verifiers, large only for a single recall-aggressive model that already over-flags in its own regime (Tab. 39). For bibtex-updater, canonical metadata leaves the FPR at its in-domain level while coverage falls: out of domain the cost is coverage, not precision. Two failure modes stay specific to biomedical data—provider safety filters block ∼3%{\sim}3\% of valid biomedical citations for the Anthropic models, distinct from any verdict error—while humanities and non-English settings remain future work. Just over half the valid entries lack a DOI (53.0%53.0\% on dev_public, 55.4%55.4\% on test_public)—many ML papers are never formally published, and DBLP records for ICML, ICLR and NeurIPS carry no DOI at all—which raises the FPR of verifiers that treat a missing identifier as suspicious.

Synthetic–real gap.

Most hallucinated entries are perturbation-generated, and the real-world anchor is thin. The benchmark holds 108 real-world entries (plus 280 LLM-generated), type-skewed (55% plausible_fabrication), with 15 compound-failure entries that involved judgment calls without human inter-annotator agreement. We report an automated three-rater reliability proxy (Fleiss’ κ=0.24\kappa=0.24, fair inter-rater agreement; § H.6) that corroborates the relabel audit but does not substitute for human IAA, which remains future work. Expanding real-world coverage from retraction databases is a priority.

Temporal fragility and the calibration question.

LLM verifiers carry an implicit training-cutoff bias that we can only partly disentangle. § 4.4 measures the post-cutoff FPR rise and the later-cutoff resistance; a recall probe and a non-Anthropic late-cutoff control point away from pure memorization for Opus 4.7 (and only partly for Sonnet 4.6), but the recall measure is model-derived and residual confounds—system-prompt handling, default temperature, native-vs-OpenRouter routing—remain. We therefore read the resistance as a descriptive signal, not a causal attribution.

Controls and residual gaps.

Three controls probe the calibration-versus-contamination question, none decisive (§ F.4). (i) A recall probe on valid 2024–2025 papers is consistent with calibration over memorization for Opus 4.7 (it accepts 84%84\% of papers it cannot recall), while Sonnet 4.6’s lower FPR is partly recall-driven. (ii) A third-provider late-cutoff control (DeepSeek-V4-Pro) also holds its post-cutoff FPR low relative to the over-flagging cohort (0.360.36 vs. 0.930.93 for GPT-5.1 on the same n=300n{=}300 subsample, at full coverage), though its cutoff matches rather than exceeds the Anthropic pair’s (§ F.4). (iii) GPT-5.1’s run-to-run variance is small (F1 std 0.0020.002 over three runs), so single-run rankings seem to be stable to sampling noise, at least for some models. The open gaps: the cross-provider control is a single third-party model, a native-API replication of the Anthropic runs is outstanding, and contamination is reduced but not fully excluded even for Opus 4.7.

Compute and token budget.

Compute caps the coverage of reasoning-mode and extended-thinking variants. Reasoning models cost far more per entry (DeepSeek-R1 at a median ∼19{\sim}19 s vs. 11–1010 s, Tab. 19), so we did not run extended-thinking variants on the full benchmark (Fig. 7 maps where their JSON-output contract holds), the agentic harness is capped at five tool calls per entry, and HaRC/verify-citations are excluded because neither produces its own verdicts at benchmark scale (§ B.2.2).

Regime conditionality and co-design.

The “FPR decides” framing is calibrated to the reviewer-bound venue-audit regime: low prevalence, finite reviewer attention, a false alarm cheap to dismiss. The PPV ranking is itself prevalence-invariant—sweeping prevalence over 11–5%5\% does not reorder the tools (Tab. 24)—so what changes across regimes is whether any verifier reaches a usable absolute precision and the cost asymmetry cFN/cFPc_{\text{FN}}/c_{\text{FP}}; under high prevalence or a high cost of a missed fabrication, recall and human triage regain primacy. Separately, bibtex-updater and the taxonomy were developed in parallel, so the taxonomy reflects fundamental verification steps but the construct-overfitting risk is non-zero; we report it as a co-designed reference (§ G.2). A second co-design channel runs through the valid-entry inclusion rule, and it is arguably stronger than the taxonomy: § 3.2 admits a valid entry only after confirming DOI resolution, title existence in at least two databases, and author–venue consistency, so every valid entry is database-confirmable by construction, and FPR—the axis we rank on—is computed on exactly that half. The rule therefore favors database-lookup architectures structurally, independently of how the taxonomy was derived. What bounds the effect is that it does not decide the outcome: an independent parametric verifier matches it: Gemini 2.5 Pro’s FPR (.050.050) is level with the co-designed tool’s (.051.051). Whether rankings on synthetic hallucinations predict performance on real errors remains open (Hardt, 2026); the 108 real-world entries are an initial signal, and the codebase tracks the number of times the dev split has been evaluated against during development, an adaptive-data-analysis hygiene measure that bounds the overfitting introduced by repeatedly reusing the same held-out set (Dwork et al., 2015).

Source availability is a second measurement condition.

Every number a retrieval-dependent verifier produces is conditional on whether the databases answered, and we report none of that conditioning per row. It is not a small effect. Holding tool and split fixed and correcting only the source conditions—keys, credentials and a 20-per-minute pace—moved the fraction of entries with at least one lookup that never completed from 53.7%53.7\% to 10.0%10.0\%, and the run got faster rather than slower, 2.42.4 s per entry against 5.75.7: a starved source turns into a retry storm that costs more than the wait it avoids. On a 119-entry probe holding model and prompt fixed, 12%12\% of flags cleared with arXiv starved against 24%24\% with it answering: the same verifier on the same entries, half the corrections. Nothing in this paper controls for it: our rows were collected under whatever the sources were doing that day, which bounds how exactly any of them can be reproduced, and we flag it as an evaluation condition that citation-verification benchmarks, ours included, do not yet report.

Endpoint drift and reproducibility.

Several ablations and the two Anthropic risk–coverage curves were collected against the OpenRouter API on a dated snapshot that does not reproduce the main-run aggregates. The Anthropic endpoints drift over time, and for these two models the drift is large enough to dominate several of the effects we measure. Two independently collected later runs agree on its direction and rough size: an OpenRouter snapshot puts Opus 4.7 at 0.072→0.1620.072{\to}0.162 and Sonnet 4.6 at 0.127→0.1650.127{\to}0.165, and the 2026-09-02 re-run lands at 0.1540.154 and 0.1610.161 (Tab. 29). Both roughly double the May FPR under a fixed model ID, prompt, split, temperature and seed. That re-run also persists per-entry predictions, which the original main run did not, so the Sonnet/Opus coverage cells and dev confidence intervals are now recoverable and are reported rather than marked “n/a”. Our convention follows from the size of the drift rather than from a preference for either collection. Cross-sectional comparisons take the latest run, so Tab. 1 reports 2026-09-02 for these two rows. Any comparison whose quantity is a difference stays inside one collection, because a 1313 pp endpoint shift swamps the differences at stake: the post-cutoff shift in Tab. 28 is under 11 pp for both models, so those rows remain wholly on May, and the agentic-inflation ratio of failure mode (i) is likewise quoted within May. Mixing the two would not merely add noise, it would report drift as a finding—pairing a September 21–23 FPR with a May 24–25 one yields −4.1-4.1 and −8.1-8.1 pp, i.e. apparent improvement on post-cutoff papers. Rankings are the more robust reading in any case, since drift shifts absolute FPR in the same direction across models while largely preserving their order (cross-regime ranking at Spearman ρ=0.90\rho{=}0.90 under prompt perturbation, § H.2). Within-run deltas (prompt-variant, field-LOO, rater-agreement) difference conditions measured against the same endpoint on the same day and so survive the drift. The released corpus is pinned at tag v1.2.0, carrying the ground-truth audit of § A.3.77 7 Later data releases (v1.2.1, v1.2.2) replace stale generation-pipeline explanation strings with diagnoses verified against CrossRef/arXiv/DBLP records (per-entry fix log in the repository); labels, hallucination types, tiers, sub-tests, and split membership are byte-identical to v1.2.0. Tag v1.2.3 additionally retypes four entries to plausible_fabrication/Tier 3 (ffe715a15b16 from fabricated_doi and ec01d96455e0 from preprint_as_published on dev_public; ab9c13051a56 and cad998c28243 from placeholder_authors on test_public) and moves the baseline results to data/v1.2/. Split membership and valid/hallucinated labels are unchanged, so aggregate DR, FPR and F1 are unaffected; the per-type and per-tier counts in this paper are those of v1.2.3.

Diagnostic resolution is lower than six.

Three of the six sub-tests carry little discriminative load on this corpus. Cross-database agreement is expected-fail for all 14 hallucination types and expected-pass for every valid entry, so it separates the two classes perfectly and localizes nothing; fields_complete is expected-fail for no type and varies only for plausible_fabrication; and doi_resolves is not applicable, or varies by entry, for seven of the fourteen (Tab. 2). The effective number of sub-tests that discriminate between hallucination types is therefore nearer three than six, which bounds how finely a failure signature can attribute an error and is a target for the next taxonomy revision.

Appendix J Broader impact and deployment safeguards

Hallmark supports scientific integrity by enabling systematic comparison of citation-verification tools, informing venue deployment as LLM-assisted writing becomes standard. A taxonomy of hallucination types could theoretically aid adversaries, but the defensive value of understanding these types outweighs the risk; the taxonomy is derived from publicly documented incidents, not novel attack research. The benchmark is open-source (MIT) and GPU-free, running on a single CPU regardless of institutional resources.

Intended use, and two uses we advise against.

Hallmark is a diagnostic for tool builders and venue operators: it measures which verifier fails on which citation error, and at what precision cost. It is not built for autonomous rejection of submissions, nor for screening authors for research misconduct, and we advise against both. Both inferences require establishing intent, which no verifier in this evaluation attempts and no metadata check can support: a flag means the metadata did not resolve against the databases queried, not that an author fabricated anything. Our own measurements are the argument against automating the decision. At a venue-realistic ∼2%{\sim}2\% base rate the best verifiers in the cohort catch one true hallucination per 6–10 flags and the most aggressive fewer than one in 35 (Tab. 23), so no operating point we measured would make an automated gate defensible.

Deployment safeguards.

Three safeguards follow from those measurements rather than from principle. A human decides: a verifier’s output routes an entry to a reviewer for checking and never stands as a verdict on the citation. A flag arrives with its evidence—which databases were queried and what each returned—so that an author can rebut it without reverse-engineering the tool. And an appeal route exists and is cheap: an author who supplies a resolving identifier or a canonical database record clears the flag without adjudication, which is the correct outcome for the recency and indexing failures below, where the tool is wrong and the citation is fine.

Who a false positive lands on.

False alarms are not distributed evenly across authors, and the unevenness is measurable rather than speculative. Averaged over the eighteen verifiers with released per-entry predictions, FPR orders the five venues identically on both public splits—ICML 0.440.44, ICLR 0.360.36, NeurIPS 0.320.32, AAAI 0.130.13, CVPR 0.090.09—and the mean pairwise Spearman correlation between verifiers’ per-venue rates is +0.56+0.56, so the burden is a property of the corpus rather than of any one tool. What the ordering tracks is bibliographic completeness, not venue standing: no valid ICML, ICLR or NeurIPS entry in the public splits carries a DOI, against every entry at CVPR and AAAI. Per-verifier spread across those venues runs from 1.31.3 pp for Gemini 2.5 Pro and 6.36.3 pp for bibtex-updater to 69.569.5 pp for GPT-5.1 and 93.993.9 pp for the agentic harness, so a low-FPR verifier also buys uniformity, while an aggressive operating point concentrates its errors on whoever is least well indexed. Publication recency behaves as a cliff rather than a gradient: within 2021–2023 no verifier’s year-to-year spread exceeds 1919 pp, but on the 35 real February-2026 arXiv preprints in the corpus—post-cutoff for every model evaluated—all eighteen verifiers over-flag and fifteen reach FPR 1.0001.000, and on the 448-entry 2024–2025 supplement all twelve LLMs are worse on 2025 than on 2024 (§§ 4.4 and F.1). The authors most exposed are therefore those publishing recent work and work whose venue records carry no resolvable identifier, which is close to the inverse of who can most easily absorb the cost. A venue that deploys a verifier without first measuring its own subgroup false-positive rates will impose this burden without observing it.

Scope of the evidence.

The conclusions here are established on English-language BibTeX from five ML venues (2021–2023), extended by a 500-entry cross-domain split covering biomedical and non-ML computer-science sources and by an authentic-LLM-output supplement spanning 42 multidisciplinary topics (§§ G.2 and C.6). They are not established for non-English citation practices, for humanities conventions where monographs and archival sources dominate, or for fields whose canonical identifiers differ from the DOI/arXiv pair these tools query. Deploying a verifier in those settings requires re-measuring its false-positive rate there first, and this benchmark does not license the transfer.
